title: Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks of teaching. Compared with a static digital textbook, the proposed system increased the unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, raised the average score for speaking tasks by 10.8 points, and reduced the teacher's correction time by 31.6%. Therefore, an AI-driven textbook can maintain the stability of the curriculum while providing personalised learning paths, rich practice materials and traceable classroom data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and tests an AI-driven practical English textbook that adaptively personalizes learning and significantly improves student performance and reduces teacher workload compared with a static digital textbook.
AI.motivation: Traditional applied English textbooks, even in digital form, present fixed content sequences that cannot adapt to individual learners’ needs, provide limited formative feedback, and offer little support for teachers in monitoring and managing classroom learning. With the rise of artificial intelligence, there is an opportunity to redesign textbooks as adaptive systems that can diagnose learner status, recommend targeted tasks, and streamline assessment, while still aligning with established curricula.
AI.method: The authors design an AI-driven practical English textbook based on a five-layer architecture: (1) knowledge mapping to structure linguistic and skill-related content; (2) learner profiling to continuously diagnose learner abilities and preferences; (3) task generation to algorithmically assemble suitable learning activities; (4) feedback orchestration to deliver timely, formative, and possibly automated feedback; and (5) teacher-side governance to give teachers oversight, control, and data analytics. They implement a prototype and conduct an eight-week teaching experiment with 186 non-English-major undergraduates, comparing outcomes against a static digital textbook condition.
AI.result: In the experimental comparison with a static digital textbook, the AI-driven textbook led to higher unit completion accuracy (improvement from 72.4% to 84.9%), an increase of 10.8 points in average scores for speaking tasks, and a 31.6% reduction in teachers’ correction time. These metrics suggest both learning gains for students and efficiency gains for teachers.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that an AI-driven, five-layer textbook architecture can preserve the stability and structure of an existing English curriculum while delivering personalized learning paths, diverse and abundant practice opportunities, and detailed, traceable learning data for classroom management. This approach demonstrates that textbooks can evolve into adaptive learning systems that simultaneously enhance learner outcomes and reduce teacher workload.

title: MasterControl Seventeen Every Time
summary: We study a governed approach to enterprise analytics: a language model interprets the question, while deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program that returns both results and evidence. We show that this restriction can remain expressive within a defined analytical class, using relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules also make results replayable. Across 440 runs, three 8B models generated SQL and selected tools at runtime, while Qwen3-8B interpreted intent only and policy executed the approved program. None of 330 runtime-planning episodes matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets; the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 of 110. This is a configuration-specific result, not evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under other designs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a governed, policy-based approach to enterprise analytics where language models only interpret questions and a deterministic policy selects from pre-approved analytical programs, ensuring reliability and replayability.
AI.motivation: Enterprise analytics needs both the flexibility of language models for interpreting natural language questions and the reliability, auditability, and governance of deterministic analytical pipelines. Existing runtime-planning agents that directly generate and execute SQL or tools can be brittle, hard to govern, and may fail to produce fully correct, auditable results.
AI.method: The authors define a governed analytical framework in which: (1) a language model maps user questions to intents within a predefined analytical class; (2) a deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program built from relational operations, aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity; and (3) the system returns both answers and supporting evidence with fixed semantics and execution rules. They experimentally compare three 8B-parameter models that generate SQL and select tools at runtime versus a Qwen3-8B model that only interprets intent while a policy executes the approved program, over 440 evaluation runs and 330 runtime-planning episodes.
AI.result: In 330 episodes where models had to plan and execute at runtime (generating SQL and selecting tools), none of the three 8B models consistently fulfilled the full "answer plus evidence" contract across all test datasets. In contrast, when Qwen3-8B was restricted to intent interpretation and a deterministic policy ran pre-approved analytical programs, the system achieved 110 out of 110 successful matches to the required answer-and-evidence specification. This demonstrates the robustness of the governed approach within the tested configuration.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested setting, a governed, policy-executed analytics framework can reliably produce correct, replayable answer-and-evidence outputs, outperforming free-form runtime-planning agents that directly generate and execute analytical code. However, the authors stress that this is a configuration-specific observation and does not prove that runtime agents cannot succeed under different designs, leaving room for further exploration of alternative architectures.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

AI.tldr: They propose Speculative Macro Commit (SMC), a system that uses a fast drafter model to pre-execute multi-step tool calls and then commit them when confirmed by a larger actor model, significantly reducing agent latency while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents are slow not only because of model inference time but also due to serial tool calls and environment interactions, which introduce wall-clock latency. Existing speculative methods mostly focus on single-step lookahead and fail to fully exploit recurring multi-step patterns in agent behavior. The paper aims to reduce end-to-end latency by reusing multi-step speculative execution without hurting task performance.
AI.method: They design a two-tier agent architecture with an authoritative large model (actor) and a smaller, faster drafter model. During execution, the drafter runs ahead on an isolated snapshot of the environment, predicting and executing future action chains. From training traces, they mine frequently recurring multi-action “skeletons” and store them as macros in a library. At runtime, they match the drafter’s predicted action chains to these macros; when the next real action chosen by the actor matches the first action of the drafted chain, the system performs a Speculative Macro Commit, directly committing the remaining pre-executed actions and their observations into the official trajectory, thus skipping their real-time execution. They compare against a sequential baseline and a single-step Speculative Actions (SA) baseline on benchmarks like τ^2-Bench Telecom and AppWorld using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as actor and Qwen3.5-4B as drafter.
AI.result: On τ^2-Bench Telecom, SMC preserves the overall task accuracy of a standard sequential agent while reducing latency by 10.23% compared to the Speculative Actions baseline and by 18.59% compared to pure sequential execution. On the more complex AppWorld benchmark, SMC reduces wall-clock time by 7.7% relative to SA and by 44.9% relative to sequential execution, with only a small drop in task completion rate. These results show that multi-step speculative macro execution provides additional speedups over existing single-step speculative methods.
AI.conclusion: SMC demonstrates that learned, reusable macro-level action patterns can be exploited to amortize the cost of multi-step speculative execution in LLM agents. By combining a fast drafter model, mined action skeletons, and a commit mechanism aligned with an authoritative actor model, SMC yields substantial wall-clock latency reductions beyond what single-step speculative actions offer, while maintaining comparable accuracy in many settings. This provides a practical runtime technique for speeding up tool-using LLM agents and suggests that further work on structured, multi-step speculation could unlock even larger gains.

title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the records that can affect the pending external action, replanning once or blocking when validation is incomplete. In 30 controlled live workflows with a post-plan revision, a freshness-only executor acts on the obsolete plan in every task, whereas PlanFence completes all tasks without an invalid action. Controlled replay reveals two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, while PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace grows. These are controlled safety and systems-cost results, not general task-accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode in distributed LLM-agent systems—executing actions based on outdated plans despite fresh state—and proposes PlanFence, a protocol that ties each action to the specific state dependencies it was planned on, validating them just-in-time to prevent stale-plan execution.
AI.motivation: Distributed teams of LLM agents share state via public records, but simply ensuring that each agent reads the latest state (state freshness) is not enough to guarantee that their current plans remain valid when state changes. An agent may commit a new requirement after a plan is formed, and another agent may execute the old plan without noticing the change, leading to invalid or unsafe external actions. The authors aim to formally characterize this "stale-plan execution" problem and provide a principled mechanism to prevent it without incurring excessive coordination cost in dynamic, high-churn environments.
AI.method: The authors define the notion of stale-plan execution and design PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans explicitly reference the precise public records (requirements, facts) used in their derivation. Before executing an external action, an executor validates only those records whose changes could affect that specific action; if validation cannot be completed or reveals inconsistency, the system either replans or blocks execution. They run 30 controlled live workflows in which the shared state is revised after planning, comparing a baseline "freshness-only" execution model against PlanFence. They also conduct controlled replays to study coordination behavior across varying levels of state churn and keyspace size.
AI.result: In the 30 live workflows with post-planning revisions, the baseline freshness-only executor always proceeds with obsolete plans, resulting in invalid actions in every task. In contrast, PlanFence completes all workflows without performing any invalid external action. The controlled replay experiments reveal that proactive synchronization strategies have lower coordination stalls at low churn, but as churn increases, PlanFence scales better by avoiding repeated coordination along update paths and by not revalidating or synchronizing over unrelated parts of the shared state as the keyspace enlarges.
AI.conclusion: PlanFence effectively prevents stale-plan execution in distributed LLM-agent teams by binding each action to the exact state dependencies used during planning and validating them just in time. While the approach imposes certain coordination overheads, it avoids unnecessary validation of unrelated state and scales better under high-churn and large keyspaces than naive synchronization strategies. The authors emphasize that their contributions are guarantees about safety and system-level coordination costs, not improvements in overall task accuracy, and position PlanFence as a principled mechanism for safe external action in multi-agent LLM workflows.

title: Where Does Harness-Optimization Value Live? Localized Gains and the Budget-Splitting Trap in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
summary:
A growing body of work improves frozen large language models (LLMs) as agents by evolving their harness: the textual scaffolding around the model, including persona, strategy, format rules, and control heuristics. Existing reflective prompt-evolution methods usually optimize this harness as one flat string. We instead ask where the optimization value actually resides. We introduce HARNESSEVO, which decomposes the harness into four separately evolvable slots: role, task-strategy, tool/format-rules, and reflection/control. Using the same reflective optimizer under an iso-budget setting, we pair this decomposition with leave-one-in and leave-one-out attribution to measure the contribution of each slot.
  On ALFWorld with a frozen 7B backbone, HARNESSEVO does not significantly improve the overall binary success rate over either the stock harness or flat-string evolution: 0.657 versus 0.642 and 0.642, respectively. However, the slot-level analysis reveals that nearly all useful optimization value is localized in the reflection/control slot, which achieves a leave-one-in gain of +0.119. The other slots are individually null. We further show that uniform budget splitting is harmful: allocating 64 rollouts across four slots leaves only 16 per slot, below the optimizer's effective search floor, causing every slot to freeze at its empty seed. Concentrating the budget on the high-credit control slot recovers the lost gain, reaching 0.761 with half the split budget.
  The effect is task-contingent. On WebShop, all slots freeze empty and all methods tie, indicating a genuine absence of recurrent, verbalizable control failures rather than budget starvation. Overall, our results suggest that harness value is localized, uniform budget splitting can be actively harmful, and credit assignment should precede structured agent-evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies where optimization value lies when evolving prompts (harnesses) for frozen LLM agents, finding that most gains come from reflection/control instructions rather than other prompt components, and that naive uniform budget splitting across components can hurt performance.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats the whole agent harness (persona, strategy, formatting, control) as a single flat string in prompt optimization, leaving unclear which parts actually matter and how to allocate limited optimization budget. This paper aims to decompose the harness and identify which components contribute to performance, to guide more efficient and principled agent evolution.
AI.method: The authors propose HARNESSEVO, which decomposes the harness into four distinct, separately optimizable slots: role, task-strategy, tool/format-rules, and reflection/control. Using the same reflective prompt-evolution optimizer and a fixed total budget of rollouts, they (1) evolve all slots jointly, (2) perform leave-one-in and leave-one-out attribution analyses to estimate each slot's contribution, and (3) study the impact of different budget allocation schemes across slots. Experiments are conducted on ALFWorld and WebShop using a frozen 7B LLM backbone.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, HARNESSEVO's overall success rate is similar to both the stock harness and flat-string evolution (around 0.65), but attribution analysis shows that nearly all meaningful performance gains come from the reflection/control slot, which yields a +0.119 gain when included alone, while other slots individually provide no measurable benefit. Splitting the optimization budget uniformly across all four slots reduces per-slot rollouts below the optimizer's effective search threshold, causing all slots to remain at their initial (empty) seeds and eliminating gains; focusing the budget on the high-credit control slot restores and improves performance up to 0.761 with only half of the uniformly split budget. On WebShop, all slots remain empty and all methods perform similarly, suggesting there are no recurrent, verbalizable control failures for optimization to exploit.
AI.conclusion: Harness optimization value is highly localized, particularly in reflection/control instructions for ALFWorld, while role, strategy, and formatting slots may contribute little under the tested setup. Uniformly splitting an optimization budget across harness components can actively harm performance by starving each component of sufficient search, so effective credit assignment and targeted budget allocation should precede structured, multi-slot agent evolution. The task-dependent nature of these findings (e.g., null effects on WebShop) implies that not all environments offer the same opportunities for harness-level control improvements.

title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) teaching assistants powered by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable educational support but often provide limited personalization. This study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework for personalizing general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants such as Jill Watson across academic disciplines and courses. The framework adapts responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding, yielding 96 distinct learner profiles. Student queries are additionally analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity at the interaction level. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts that condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. The framework is evaluated through experiments using NLP metrics and a human study with five participants. Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions, with statistical analyses identifying learner attributes associated with measurable response changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prompt-engineering framework to personalize LLM-based AI teaching assistants along six learner dimensions and interaction-level cognitive complexity, showing that structured prompts can adapt response style and behavior without retraining.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM-based AI teaching assistants scale well but lack individualized support; the paper is motivated by the need for systematic, low-cost personalization across disciplines and courses, without retraining or fine-tuning models.
AI.method: The authors design a prompt-engineering framework that encodes six learner-specific attributes—self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding—forming 96 learner profiles. Student queries are classified using Bloom's Taxonomy to infer cognitive complexity. These attributes and assessments are embedded as structured control metadata in prompts to condition an LLM or LLM+RAG system. They then evaluate via NLP metrics and a small human user study with five participants, comparing different personalization conditions and analyzing response differences statistically.
AI.result: The system produces responses whose style and structure vary across personalization conditions. Both automatic NLP metrics and human ratings indicate perceived and measurable differences linked to specific learner attributes, suggesting that the prompt structure meaningfully influences LLM behavior without modifying the underlying model.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based personalization of LLM teaching assistants is feasible and can induce adaptive response behavior tied to learner profiles and cognitive demand. Although findings are preliminary due to small sample size, the framework demonstrates a practical way to individualize educational AI systems across courses without retraining, and motivates further, larger-scale validation and refinement.

title: Bounded Personas Match Retrieval on Classification but Not Regression for a Frozen Agent
summary: A personalized language agent must convert a user's interaction history into behavior on each new request at inference time. Two strategies dominate. Retrieval pulls a few of the user's most relevant past items into the prompt, which is accurate but pays a per-query selection and context cost that grows with the history. Distillation instead compresses the history once into a compact natural-language persona, which is bounded, query-independent, and interpretable, but is widely assumed to sacrifice accuracy. Whether, and on which tasks, a distilled persona can match retrieval has not been characterized cleanly. We introduce PersonaLink, a training-free method that distills a user's history into a bounded three-field persona and recursively refines it: each pass self-evaluates the frozen agent on a held-out slice of the user's own labeled history, rewrites the persona from its errors, and keeps the result only when it does not regress on that slice. Because every comparison shares one frozen 7B backbone and differs only in what is placed in context, the design isolates the effect of representation from that of the model. The result is a clear task-type asymmetry. On 200 users of LaMP-2 (15-way news categorization), PersonaLink reaches 0.745-0.755 accuracy, statistically indistinguishable from BM25 retrieval (0.760-0.765).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PersonaLink, a training-free method to distill a user’s interaction history into a compact, recursively refined persona that can match retrieval-based methods on certain tasks while using bounded context.
AI.motivation: Personalized language agents need to use a user’s growing interaction history at inference time. Existing strategies trade off accuracy and efficiency: retrieval-based methods are accurate but incur increasing per-query retrieval and context costs as history grows, whereas distilled personas are efficient and interpretable but assumed to be less accurate. The authors want to understand when a distilled persona can match retrieval and design a method that maintains accuracy while keeping context bounded and query-independent.
AI.method: The authors propose PersonaLink, which distills a user’s history into a bounded, three-field natural language persona. The method is training-free and operates via recursive refinement. For each iteration, the system evaluates a frozen 7B backbone model on a held-out, labeled slice of the user’s own history using the current persona, analyzes the model’s errors, rewrites the persona to address those errors, and keeps the new persona only if performance on that slice does not regress. All comparisons use the same frozen model and differ only in what representation (retrieval vs persona) is placed into the context, cleanly isolating the effect of representation.
AI.result: On 200 users from the LaMP-2 benchmark (15-way news categorization), PersonaLink achieves 0.745–0.755 accuracy, which is statistically indistinguishable from BM25 retrieval’s 0.760–0.765 accuracy. This demonstrates that a compact, distilled persona can perform on par with retrieval-based methods on this type of task, despite using bounded context and no additional training.
AI.conclusion: A carefully constructed and recursively refined, three-field natural language persona can, in some task settings, match the performance of retrieval-based personalization while being more efficient and interpretable. By holding the backbone model fixed and varying only the representation, the study shows a clear task-type asymmetry and provides evidence that persona distillation is a viable alternative to retrieval for tasks like multi-way news categorization.

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
summary: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and measures a new failure mode in LLM moral advice called 'narrative captivity,' where models over-align with a one-sided, multi-turn story and fail to seek missing perspectives.
AI.motivation: As people increasingly use LLMs for advice on ethically sensitive interpersonal issues, it's important to understand how models behave in realistic, multi-turn consultations rather than simplified, single-turn or adversarial setups. Real conflicts often feature one-sided, self-justifying narratives and information asymmetries, so the authors want to know whether LLMs get swayed by such narratives without any explicit counter-arguments.
AI.method: The authors define 'narrative captivity' as a failure mode where the model accepts a one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator’s interpretation. They construct a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal-conflict scenarios across six moral dimensions. They then evaluate 17 LLMs by comparing their moral judgments in single-turn settings against multi-turn settings where the conflict is narrated over time by one party. They perform stage-level analyses to identify which parts of training or decoding contribute most (highlighting preference optimization) and test four different inference-time mitigation strategies.
AI.result: Narrative captivity is prevalent across the evaluated LLMs. Multi-turn, one-sided narration shifts the models’ final moral judgments by an average of 25 percentage points relative to comparable single-turn baselines, showing that narration alone significantly sways the models. Stage-level analysis implicates preference optimization as a key driver of this susceptibility, while the four tested inference-time strategies only partially reduce the effect and do not fully resolve it.
AI.conclusion: LLMs currently used for everyday moral advice are vulnerable to being unduly influenced by one-sided, multi-turn narratives, leading them to adopt the narrator’s framing instead of maintaining independent judgment or seeking missing perspectives. Preference optimization appears to exacerbate this issue, and current inference-time mitigations are insufficient. The authors argue that future LLM advisor design should explicitly address narrative captivity so models better preserve independent, balanced judgment in real-world moral consultations.

title: Counterexamples as Feedback for Agent Self-Correction
summary: Single-turn code-generation metrics understate a central property of deployed agents: whether they can repair a wrong artifact after receiving concrete feedback. This paper presents A-CEGIS, a lightweight framework that uses counterexamples as feedback for evaluating multi-turn refinement in natural-language-to-regex synthesis. An agent proposes a regex, a deterministic oracle checks it under full-match semantics, and compact false-positive or false-negative witnesses guide the next turn. On 30 NL-RX-Turk tasks, diagnostic counterexample feedback solves 90\% of tasks within a four-turn ablation budget, compared with 17% for zero-shot generation, 27% for generic self-correction, and 23% for error-only feedback. In a full diagnostic run with hardening, all tasks are solved on the hidden set by the final turn, with mean time-to-success of 2.7 turns and robust success of 77% after targeted probing. These results show that A-CEGIS measures how efficiently an agent improves across turns while adding a practical robustness check beyond the original held-out cases.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces A-CEGIS, a framework to evaluate and improve multi-turn natural-language-to-regex synthesis using counterexample-guided refinement, showing large gains over single-turn and naive self-correction baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing code-generation metrics focus on single-turn performance and fail to capture a key property of deployed agents: their ability to iteratively repair incorrect outputs in response to concrete feedback. In natural-language-to-regex synthesis, a realistic deployment involves multiple refinement rounds driven by examples where the current regex fails. There is a need for an evaluation framework that systematically measures how well agents use such counterexample feedback to converge to correct and robust solutions, beyond just held-out test accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose A-CEGIS, a lightweight evaluation framework inspired by counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS). In this setup, an agent receives a natural-language description and proposes a regex. A deterministic oracle then evaluates the regex under full-match semantics and returns compact counterexamples: false-positive or false-negative witness strings. The agent uses this feedback for multi-turn refinement, producing improved regexes across turns. The framework is applied to 30 NL-RX-Turk tasks. Several feedback conditions are compared: zero-shot (single-turn) generation, generic self-correction, error-only feedback, and full diagnostic counterexample feedback. The authors also run a full diagnostic setting with additional "hardening" and targeted probing to assess robustness beyond the original held-out set.
AI.result: On the 30 NL-RX-Turk tasks, diagnostic counterexample feedback in A-CEGIS solves 90% of tasks within a four-turn budget, a substantial improvement over baselines: 17% task success for zero-shot generation, 27% for generic self-correction, and 23% for error-only feedback. In a full diagnostic run with additional hardening, the framework achieves 100% task completion on the hidden set by the final turn, with a mean time-to-success of 2.7 turns. Under targeted probing to stress-test robustness, 77% of tasks remain successfully solved, indicating that most learned regexes generalize beyond the initial evaluation cases.
AI.conclusion: A-CEGIS provides an effective, lightweight way to evaluate how efficiently code-generation agents improve across multiple interaction turns using counterexample feedback. The experimental results on natural-language-to-regex synthesis show that structured diagnostic counterexamples dramatically outperform single-turn generation and naive self-correction strategies. Moreover, incorporating hardening and targeted probing offers a practical robustness check that extends beyond standard held-out test evaluations. The framework thus better reflects the behavior of deployed interactive agents and can guide the development of more robust, feedback-driven synthesis systems.

title: Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection
summary: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dude, a dual-detection multi-agent LLM system that improves automatic detection of inconsistencies between research papers and their released code, achieving notably higher recall, precision, and F1 than existing methods.
AI.motivation: As research submissions scale up, manually verifying that published papers are consistent with their associated code has become infeasible. Existing LLM-based approaches typically use a single agent with limited context capacity and can only perform one-sided discrepancy checks, leading to low recall in finding paper-code mismatches. Moreover, naive multi-agent designs suffer from over-interpretation and over-reporting, increasing false positives because paper text and code differ in granularity and expression. There is a need for an automated method that can better capture discrepancies while controlling false alarms.
AI.method: The authors propose Dude, a Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. Instead of a single LLM agent, Dude employs two detection agents that analyze both paper and code, and then interact. The key technical contributions are: (1) a granularity-aligned negotiation mechanism that reconciles the differing levels of detail and representation between natural language descriptions in the paper and programming language in the code to reduce misinterpretations; and (2) a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism that filters and prioritizes only the most salient and well-supported discrepancy candidates, preventing agents from over-reporting inconsistencies. These mechanisms are built on top of LLM agents and are evaluated on real-world datasets of paper-code pairs.
AI.result: On real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets, Dude significantly outperforms baseline single-agent and naive multi-agent LLM methods. It improves recall and precision by up to 22.8% and yields F1 score gains of up to 18.7%, indicating that it both finds more true discrepancies and reduces false positives compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Dude demonstrates that a dual-detection, multi-agent LLM architecture with granularity-aligned negotiation and salience filtering can substantially improve automatic paper-code discrepancy detection over existing single-agent paradigms. Aligning the granularity between paper language and code language and carefully filtering reported issues are crucial to achieving both higher recall and precision in this emerging task.

title: Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection
summary: Linear probes can be used to detect behaviors and concepts inside language model activations, but may fail to transfer to out-of-distribution examples. When studying the generalization performance of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes over 3 held-out deception detection datasets, we find that projecting inputs onto a small subset of principal components (PCs) from the training distribution of activations enables cross-domain transfer that nearly matches the performance of probes trained directly on the test distribution. Furthermore, we find that PC interpretations can be used to find a subset of those transferable PCs. By using an LLM judge to score each PC on whether its most/ least activating examples imply a transferable deception direction, then probing on the highest-scoring PCs, we close the baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging. The directions a source probe weights heavily appear to encode source-specific surface features, while the directions that actually transfer appear to encode the same contrast more abstractly, in a way natural language descriptions can capture. Broadly, our results suggest that the OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that selecting appropriate principal component subspaces of language model activations dramatically improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of linear probes for deception detection, nearly matching in-domain performance.
AI.motivation: Linear probes can detect conceptual features in language model activations but often fail to generalize across domains (OOD). The authors aim to understand and improve why probes trained on one deception dataset perform poorly on others, and to determine what properties of the representation space control OOD robustness.
AI.method: They train linear probes on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct activations for deception detection, then evaluate on three held-out deception datasets. They apply PCA to activations from the training distribution, project inputs onto a selected subset of principal components, and train/evaluate probes in this reduced subspace. They interpret PCs by examining examples that strongly activate or de-activate each PC and use an LLM judge to score whether these patterns indicate a dataset-agnostic notion of deception. They then restrict probing to the PCs with high transferability scores and compare performance to probes trained directly on the target domains (oracle) and standard full-space probes (baseline).
AI.result: Projecting onto a small subset of training-distribution PCs significantly improves cross-domain transfer, with performance close to probes trained on the target distribution. Using LLM-based interpretations to select only those PCs whose examples reflect transferable, abstract deception signals closes 78% of the performance gap on the Insider Trading Report dataset and 25% on Sandbagging relative to an oracle probe. Analysis shows that heavily weighted directions in source-only probes capture source-specific surface features, while the PCs that transfer encode more abstract contrasts that align with natural language descriptions.
AI.conclusion: Out-of-distribution robustness of linear probes on language model activations is largely governed by which representation subspace they operate in. Careful subspace selection, especially via principal components linked to abstract, interpretable concepts of deception, enables much better cross-domain generalization than naive full-space probing and can approach the performance of in-domain-trained probes.

title: DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval: Evaluating Implicit Instruction Following in Full-Duplex Voice Agents
summary: Full-duplex voice agents must continuously decide when to listen, backchannel, interrupt, handle speech overlaps, take the floor, and yield. Existing benchmarks largely test these behaviors through explicit turn-management instructions, while deployed agents are often configured through roles or personas from which the appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. (DSB-IFEval) comprises 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols for instruction-following: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona--rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. We measure real-time floor management using a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) and persona-consistent content using LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS). Across six real-time speech systems, we find architecture-dependent trade-offs. Full duplex models like F-Actor and PersonaPlex are more sensitive to whether conversational behavior is stated explicitly or must be inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5%, respectively, under persona-only conditioning. In contrast, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content, but their floor behavior does not adapt across explicit and persona-only instructions and remains constrained on several proactive actions. We further find that even if systems reliably follow conflicting directives to their prescribed persona, they still struggle to override them under safety conflict. These results show that inferring the behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.

AI.tldr: They build a benchmark (DSB-IFEval) to test how real-time, full-duplex voice agents implicitly follow conversational instructions derived from roles/personas rather than only explicit rules.
AI.motivation: Real deployed voice agents must manage turn-taking and behavior implicitly from roles/personas and overlapping speech, but existing benchmarks mostly test explicit, text-based turn-taking instructions, missing realistic, implicit instruction-following in full-duplex, real-time settings.
AI.method: They design DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval with 1,038 spoken test cases across eight assistant roles and five conditioning protocols (default, explicit rules, persona-only, persona+rules, and conflicting instructions). They evaluate multiple real-time speech systems with two metrics: a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) for floor-management behavior and an LLM-based Persona Adherence Score (PAS) for content consistency with persona.
AI.result: Across six systems, they observe architecture-dependent tradeoffs: some full duplex models (e.g., F-Actor, PersonaPlex) are highly sensitive to whether behavior is given explicitly or only via persona, with significantly lower adherence under persona-only conditioning, while others (e.g., GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, Fun-Audio-Chat) maintain persona-consistent content but do not adapt their floor behavior to persona vs explicit instructions and are limited in proactive behaviors. Systems that can follow conflicting instructions in line with persona still fail to reliably override personas when safety conflicts arise.
AI.conclusion: Implicitly inferring behavior from roles/personas, executing the correct behavior at the right conversational moment, and resolving conflicts between behavior rules, personas, and safety constraints are distinct and unsolved challenges for full-duplex voice agents, highlighting the need for better models and evaluation of real-time instruction-following and floor management.

title: R$^{2}$Adapter: A Routing and Rewriting Adapter for Efficient Hybrid RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a prevailing paradigm for enhancing Large Language Models (LLMs) with non-parametric knowledge. Vanilla RAG efficiently handles simple queries but struggles with relational or multi-hop reasoning. Graph-based RAG alleviates this issue but incurs higher inference complexity and latency. In practice, user queries can differ significantly in their complexity, rendering a fixed RAG strategy suboptimal. However, existing hybrid text-graph RAG methods typically rely on heuristic and LLM-based routing, resulting in unnecessary overhead and strong dependence on the underlying LLM. To address these challenges, we propose R$^{2}$Adapter, a lightweight plug-in Routing and Rewriting Adapter designed to allocate queries between vanilla and graph-based RAG dynamically. By routing only the queries that genuinely benefit from graph-based reasoning, R$^{2}$Adapter reduces unnecessary graph retrieval overhead. Additionally, uncertain graph-routed queries are rewritten to better expose their multi-hop reasoning requirements, improving retrieval quality without additional supervision. Extensive experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that R$^{2}$Adapter reduces graph-based RAG usage by up to 59% while maintaining comparable answer accuracy. This adapter is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into diverse vanilla and graph-based RAG pipelines, providing an efficient and adaptive solution for hybrid RAG systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces R^2Adapter, a lightweight routing and rewriting module that dynamically chooses between vanilla and graph-based RAG, cutting graph usage by up to 59% while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Vanilla RAG is efficient but poor at relational/multi-hop reasoning, while graph-based RAG improves reasoning but is slow and costly. Real user queries vary in complexity, so a single fixed RAG strategy is inefficient. Existing hybrid text-graph RAG systems rely on heuristic or LLM-based routing, which adds overhead and ties performance to a specific LLM. The authors want an adaptive, efficient, and model-agnostic way to decide when to use graph-based reasoning and how to better formulate complex queries.
AI.method: They design R^2Adapter, a plug-in module with two main functions: (1) routing: it predicts whether a query should use vanilla RAG or graph-based RAG, sending only truly complex/multi-hop queries to the graph pipeline to save cost; (2) rewriting: for queries routed to the graph pipeline but with high uncertainty, it rewrites them to explicitly reveal multi-hop/relational requirements, improving graph retrieval. The adapter is lightweight, model-agnostic, and can sit on top of different vanilla and graph-based RAG pipelines without extra supervision for the rewriting step.
AI.result: Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks, R^2Adapter reduces the use of graph-based RAG by up to 59% while keeping answer accuracy comparable to always using graph-based RAG. This shows it can significantly lower retrieval overhead and latency without sacrificing performance.
AI.conclusion: R^2Adapter provides an efficient, adaptive control layer for hybrid RAG systems, automatically routing and rewriting queries to balance cost and performance. It enables practical deployment of hybrid vanilla/graph RAG by reducing unnecessary graph retrieval while preserving multi-hop reasoning quality, and can be easily integrated into diverse RAG pipelines because it is model-agnostic and lightweight.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark and analysis of when GUI agents should terminate instead of executing infeasible or conflicting natural-language instructions, and proposes CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that improves agents’ ability to detect and safely stop in such cases while preserving normal performance.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agents focus on executing instructions but not on handling infeasible or self-contradictory instructions that real users may give by mistake. This leads to overcompliance: agents keep acting even when instructions conflict with themselves or with the visible GUI state, which is unsafe and unreliable. The authors aim to systematically study and reduce this overcompliant behavior by giving agents a notion of when *not* to act.
AI.method: The authors construct CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark that includes two types of conflicts: (1) conflicts within the instruction text itself, and (2) conflicts between the instruction and the actual GUI context. They then propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that wraps around existing GUI agents. CONFLICTGUARD has two key components: a feasibility verification protocol that explicitly makes the agent reason about instruction logic and GUI evidence before taking actions, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that, based on the feasibility assessment, either lets the agent act normally or modulates behavior toward terminating safely instead of executing conflicting steps.
AI.result: On five popular GUI agents, evaluation on CONFLICTGUI shows that baseline agents exhibit strong execution-biased overcompliance, frequently performing actions even when instructions are conflicting or infeasible. With CONFLICTGUARD applied at inference time, the average success rate on conflict tasks increases substantially, while performance on standard feasible GUI tasks remains largely unchanged, indicating minimal overhead or degradation in normal operation.
AI.conclusion: Conflict-aware termination is a critical yet overlooked capability for GUI agents. The proposed CONFLICTGUI benchmark exposes widespread overcompliance in existing systems, and the CONFLICTGUARD framework demonstrates that a lightweight, model-agnostic inference-time intervention can significantly improve agents’ ability to detect conflicts and refrain from unnecessary or harmful actions, all without sacrificing performance on regular tasks.

title: BharatGather: A Culturally-Informed Benchmark Dataset for Misinformation and Fake News Detection in Indian Public Events
summary: Large-scale public events, such as religious festivals, political rallies, and cultural gatherings, are increasingly vulnerable to the rapid dissemination of misinformation, posing substantial risks to public safety and social cohesion. While automated fake news detection has seen significant methodological progress, existing benchmarks frequently fail to capture the socio-cultural nuances and event-specific dynamics characteristic of the Indian context. This paper introduces BharatGather, a curated, multi-source dataset specifically engineered for binary misinformation classification within the ecosystem of Indian mass gatherings. The corpus comprises 14,646 records constructed through a hybrid pipeline involving systematic web scraping of prominent fact-checking platforms, multimedia transcript extraction, and Large Language Model (LLM)-mediated synthetic augmentation to ensure narrative diversity. By providing a resource tailored to the unique complexities of event-aware misinformation in India, this work facilitates the development of culturally informed detection systems and establishes a rigorous benchmark for evaluating their performance in high-stakes public environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces BharatGather, a dataset for binary misinformation detection around Indian mass gatherings.
AI.motivation: Large-scale public events in India are vulnerable to fast-spreading misinformation, but existing fake news benchmarks do not capture Indian socio-cultural and event-specific nuances, limiting the effectiveness of detection models in this high-stakes context.
AI.method: Curate a 14,646-record dataset via a hybrid pipeline: web scraping major fact-checking sites, extracting transcripts from multimedia content, and using LLM-based synthetic augmentation to enrich narrative diversity, all focused on Indian mass gatherings and labeled for binary misinformation classification.
AI.result: The outcome is BharatGather, a sizable, multi-source, culturally grounded corpus centered on misinformation around Indian public gatherings, suitable for training and benchmarking binary misinformation classifiers.
AI.conclusion: BharatGather provides a culturally and event-aware benchmark that can enable more accurate and context-sensitive misinformation detection systems for Indian mass gatherings and support rigorous evaluation in safety-critical public scenarios.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a "Fluency Trap" where people over-trust fluent AI text and under-trust accurate AI-labeled content, and proposes an evidence-visualization interface (Provenance Density) that helps users distinguish true from fabricated claims.
AI.motivation: Generative AI can produce highly fluent but potentially false text (hallucinations). People often use fluency as a shortcut for truth, leading them to trust plausible-sounding but incorrect AI outputs and to discount correct information once they know it is AI-generated. Current solutions like binary "Made with AI" labels only disclose authorship and do not help users see the evidential support behind claims. The paper aims to find a better transparency mechanism that focuses on the evidence underlying claims rather than on who or what wrote the text.
AI.method: The authors define the "Fluency Trap" problem and design an interface concept called Provenance Density, which visualizes how many claims in a text are backed by verifiable evidence. They conduct (1) a user study with 81 participants using an idealized version of this interface to test whether it improves users' ability to discern true from fabricated content, and (2) a technical audit over 200 samples to analyze what underlying technical signals (retrieval density, consistency checks, etc.) best support this visualization, especially for dynamic queries.
AI.result: In the user study, the Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication: participants exposed to it were 4.15 points better at discriminating true from false content (effect size d=1.82), whereas participants without any such signal showed no measurable ability to discriminate. In the technical audit, the authors found that simply using retrieval density as the underlying signal was not sufficient to drive good performance. Instead, a "Consistency Veto" mechanism unexpectedly contributed most of the useful discriminative signal on dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: As AI-generated text becomes as fluent as human writing, authorship labels like "Made with AI" are not enough to guide user trust. Effective transparency should shift from disclosing who wrote the text to visualizing the evidential support for its claims. Provenance Density, supported strongly by a Consistency Veto mechanism, is a promising approach to help users detect fabrications and avoid the Fluency Trap.

title: PiPMRE: A Pipeline Based on Language Model for Medical Relation Extraction
summary: Medical relation extraction (MRE) is commonly known for extracting entities and their relations jointly from a medical text, which has attracted considerable attention in recent years. Previous studies treat MRE as a sequence tagging task, which results in either a challenging design of the tagging schema or a failed extraction of multiple relations, due to intricate relationships among medical entities. In this work, we review the task from the linguistic perspective and propose a novel pipeline framework, PiPMRE, developed on language models to enhance MRE performance. Specifically, PiPMRE consists of a relation generator and a relation filter. Given a text, the generator first yields multiple relational triplets, and then the filter scores each triplet and retains only those that pass the borderline as the final results. Implementing PiPMRE requires no tagging schema; instead, we use a simple template to reformulate the input text, ensuring that entities and relations are generated in a contextual order. Extensive experimental results on two public datasets demonstrate the advancement of PiPMRE. It surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by an average of 5.6 recall points and 4.4 accuracy points. PiPMRE's superiority is also demonstrated in few-shot settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PiPMRE, a pipeline framework for medical relation extraction that avoids complex tagging schemes by using a generator–filter architecture with language models, significantly improving recall and accuracy over prior state-of-the-art, including in few-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing medical relation extraction methods usually cast the task as sequence tagging, which requires complicated tagging schemas and struggles with texts containing multiple, intertwined relations among medical entities. These limitations hinder performance and scalability, particularly given the linguistic complexity of medical narratives. The authors aim to find a linguistically grounded, simpler, and more effective approach that can better handle multiple relations and work well even with limited data.
AI.method: The authors introduce PiPMRE, a two-stage pipeline framework based on language models. First, a relation generator takes the input medical text and, using a simple template reformulation, produces multiple candidate relational triplets (entity1, relation, entity2) in the order they appear in context, without relying on any tagging schema. Second, a relation filter scores each generated triplet and discards low-confidence or spurious ones, keeping only those above a threshold. This generator–filter design is intended to leverage language models' strengths in generation while controlling noise through post-hoc filtering.
AI.result: On two public medical relation extraction datasets, PiPMRE outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving on average 5.6 percentage points higher recall and 4.4 percentage points higher accuracy. The framework also shows strong performance in few-shot learning scenarios, indicating robustness and data efficiency compared with prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: PiPMRE, a language-model-based generator–filter pipeline for medical relation extraction, alleviates the need for complex tagging schemas and better captures multiple contextual relations among medical entities. Its superior performance on benchmark datasets and in few-shot settings suggests that rethinking MRE as a generation-plus-filtering problem is a promising direction for future work in medical NLP.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: AutoGraphForge is a pipeline that automatically generates, filters, tests, and then formally proves graph-theoretic conjectures using large datasets and neural theorem provers in Lean.
AI.motivation: Automating the full research loop in graph theory—from conjecture generation to formal proof—can greatly accelerate discovery and ensure verified correctness. Existing systems often handle only parts of this loop (e.g., conjecture generation or proof search), so there is a need for an integrated, scalable pipeline working on rich graph datasets and connecting to modern proof assistants.
AI.method: The system runs in rounds. A Graffiti3-based generator proposes conjectures about graph invariants using a small evolving table T of graphs and their invariants, which is extended only by newly found counterexamples. A novelty filter containing 559 known relations, closed under transitivity and linear-identity substitution, formulates a linear program to decide if a proposed conjecture is already implied by known ones. Remaining candidates are tested against a large dataset (~348k graphs from House of Graphs, all connected graphs up to 9 vertices, extremal families, and random models). Counterexample-search algorithms further attack survivors. Conjectures that withstand this phase are automatically translated into Lean 4 statement skeletons. Two neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B) then attempt proofs, with all proofs independently checked by the Lean kernel against a fixed mathlib4 plus a custom invariant library.
AI.result: After several HPC rounds, the system produced 6,522 conjectures that survived the novelty filter, large refutation dataset, and active counterexample search. Among these are interesting new relations involving annihilation number and edge-cover number in specific graph classes, which were subsequently proved manually. The formalization/proving backend is implemented end-to-end, passes sanity checks, and is operating on the cluster.
AI.conclusion: AutoGraphForge demonstrates a working end-to-end pipeline for automated mathematical discovery in graph theory: it can generate large numbers of nontrivial, novel conjectures, subject them to extensive verification against data, then translate and attempt to formally prove them in Lean using neural provers under kernel verification. The project is ongoing but shows that integrating conjecture generation, large-scale testing, and formal proof search is practical and promising for future automated research systems.

title: Margins, Not Windows: Training-Free Per-Step Lossy Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by drafting candidate tokens and verifying them in parallel. Tree-attention drafters such as EAGLE-3 are widely adopted, yet typically hold two decisions fixed: (1) a strict token-match verification rule and (2) a static draft-tree shape. Prior work relaxes each in isolation under limiting assumptions: long draft chains for training-free lossy verification, and adaptive tree shaping under a fixed token budget. We introduce AdaptiveSpec, a training-free per-step speculative decoding method that adapts both decisions from internal signals already produced during decoding. A per-step margin rule promotes a mismatched draft-proposed token when the ratio of the target's probability on the drafted token to its top-1 probability exceeds a threshold with no dependence on draft length or underlying drafter architecture. A per-step tree policy adjusts the draft tree's depth, width, and node count directly from a fused signal of draft top-1 confidence and a rolling acceptance history capturing recent draft-target agreement, allowing the total draft count to vary rather than only be redistributed. The two adaptations operate on orthogonal axes and compound in effect. Implemented on the SGLang production-grade serving engine, AdaptiveSpec improves throughput over the state-of-the-art autoregressive speculative decoding method EAGLE-3 by up to 56%, recovering 93% to fully lossless task accuracy across GSM8K, MATH-500, and HumanEval on three target models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B).

AI.tldr: AdaptiveSpec is a training-free speculative decoding method that adaptively relaxes token verification and dynamically reshapes draft trees per step, significantly boosting LLM throughput while keeping near-lossless accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods with tree-attention drafters (e.g., EAGLE-3) use rigid design choices: strict token-match verification and fixed draft-tree shapes. Attempts to relax either are limited—lossy verification assumes long chains and adaptive trees assume fixed token budgets. There is a need for a general, training-free method that can simultaneously adapt verification and draft structure using only signals already available during decoding, to improve speed without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: AdaptiveSpec introduces two per-step adaptive mechanisms, both training-free and driven solely by internal decoding signals. (1) A per-step margin verification rule that allows accepting a drafted token even when it doesn’t exactly match the target’s top-1 prediction, provided the ratio between the target model’s probability on the drafted token and its own top-1 probability exceeds a tunable threshold; this rule is independent of draft length and drafter architecture. (2) A per-step tree policy that dynamically adjusts the speculative draft tree’s depth, width, and total number of nodes using a fused signal that combines current draft top-1 confidence with a rolling acceptance history measuring recent agreement between drafter and target; this lets the total number of drafted tokens expand or shrink instead of merely redistributing a fixed budget.
AI.result: Integrated into the SGLang production serving stack and evaluated on GSM8K, MATH-500, and HumanEval with three 8B-class target models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B), AdaptiveSpec achieves up to 56% higher throughput compared to the prior state-of-the-art autoregressive speculative decoding method EAGLE-3, while maintaining 93%–100% of the task accuracy (i.e., effectively lossless performance on these benchmarks).
AI.conclusion: By jointly and adaptively relaxing token verification and draft-tree structure on a per-step basis, without any extra training or model modifications, AdaptiveSpec compounds efficiency gains and pushes speculative decoding performance beyond EAGLE-3, delivering substantial inference speedups while preserving near-lossless accuracy across reasoning and coding benchmarks.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes NTEP, a supervision scheme that explicitly annotates which tools and evidence are necessary for answering an image-grounded question, and NTEP-R, a reward mechanism that uses these annotations to train agentic VLMs to call tools efficiently and summarize the right evidence, leading to better accuracy and fewer redundant tool calls.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic vision-language models can call tools like image cropping or web search, but their training mainly rewards getting the final answer correct. This weakly supervises how they select tools and use evidence, so models often make unnecessary or irrelevant tool calls and then fail to correctly extract and use the information they retrieved. The authors aim to directly supervise the sequence of evidence-seeking actions so models learn to plan and utilize tools in a more principled, efficient way.
AI.method: The authors introduce NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), which annotates, for each query, the minimal set of external evidence and the corresponding necessary tool calls. Based on NTEP, they design NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), which gives reward if (1) the model’s pre-call intent matches a necessary evidence-seeking goal and (2) the model’s post-call summary matches the annotated necessary evidence. They also add a non-repeated-goal regularizer that penalizes tool calls that pursue already-satisfied NTEP goals. They instantiate this framework in an 8B-parameter agentic VLM with three tools (e.g., crop, image search, text search) and train it using this reward structure.
AI.result: Across seven image-grounded benchmarks focused on search and reasoning, the NTEP-trained 8B model (NTEP-8B) achieves higher accuracy on search-oriented tasks and uses tools more efficiently than baselines. It reduces redundant and off-target tool calls and improves the quality of evidence summaries from tool observations within the unified three-tool framework.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained supervision over the entire tool-evidence path, rather than only final answers, is crucial for training robust agentic VLMs. By explicitly supervising which tools to call, when, and how to summarize their outputs, the NTEP and NTEP-R framework substantially improves both effectiveness and efficiency of tool use in vision-language reasoning agents.

title: Distilled Rapid Embedding Transfer (DRET): Parameter-Efficient Biomedical Domain Adaptation via Priority-Based Embedding Transfer
summary: Large domain-specific language models such as BioBERT and ClinicalBERT achieve strong performance on biomedical NLP tasks, but their computational demands make them impractical for many real-world deployments. General-purpose, parameter-efficient models such as DistilBERT are lightweight yet lack the domain knowledge required for specialized tasks such as PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) classification. We introduce Distilled Rapid Embedding Transfer (DRET), a knowledge-transfer paradigm that injects biomedical domain knowledge from large specialized models into a smaller general-purpose model without retraining on the original specialized corpora. DRET is developed as an iterative family of strategies: a unified tokenizer-merge strategy (DRET 1.x), hybrid embedding averaging (DRET 2.0), and a priority-based embedding-transfer mechanism (DRET 3.x) that hierarchically selects embeddings from the most authoritative source models, further combined with embedding-layer freezing, differential learning rates, label propagation, and imbalance-aware loss functions (DRET 4.x). We evaluate DRET on token-level PICO classification using the EBM-NLP corpus under severe class imbalance, across a twelve-metric battery. DRET-enhanced DistilBERT (66M parameters) attains balanced accuracy, recall, and ROC-AUC competitive with, and on several class-wise metrics exceeding, models an order of magnitude larger, while retaining DistilBERT's efficiency. We further show that transfer occurs at the embedding level through cosine-similarity, semantic-shift, and t-SNE analyses. DRET offers a scalable, resource-efficient route to near-domain-expert performance for biomedical text mining, with direct application to automated systematic literature reviews and clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DRET, a set of strategies to transfer biomedical knowledge from large domain-specific language models into a small, efficient model (DistilBERT), achieving near state-of-the-art PICO classification under class imbalance with far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Domain-specific models like BioBERT and ClinicalBERT perform very well in biomedical NLP but are too large and computationally expensive for many real-world uses.
