Lightweight models like DistilBERT are efficient but lack specialized biomedical knowledge, limiting performance on tasks such as PICO classification. There is a need for a practical way to inject domain knowledge into small models without retraining on massive specialized corpora.
AI.method: The authors introduce Distilled Rapid Embedding Transfer (DRET), an iterative family of knowledge-transfer strategies that operate primarily at the embedding level. DRET 1.x uses unified tokenizer-merge strategies to reconcile vocabularies of general and biomedical models. DRET 2.0 introduces hybrid embedding averaging that combines embeddings from multiple models. DRET 3.x adds priority-based embedding transfer, hierarchically selecting embeddings from the most authoritative source models. DRET 4.x augments these with embedding-layer freezing, differential learning rates, label propagation, and imbalance-aware loss functions. The approach transfers domain knowledge into DistilBERT without retraining on the original large biomedical corpora.
AI.result: On token-level PICO classification using the EBM-NLP corpus with severe class imbalance, DRET-enhanced DistilBERT (66M parameters) achieves balanced accuracy, recall, and ROC-AUC that are competitive with, and on several per-class metrics better than, models that are about ten times larger. Analyses based on cosine similarity, semantic shift, and t-SNE visualizations confirm that meaningful knowledge transfer occurs at the embedding level.
AI.conclusion: DRET provides a scalable, resource-efficient paradigm for injecting domain-specific biomedical knowledge into compact language models, enabling near-domain-expert performance on PICO classification while maintaining the efficiency of DistilBERT. This makes it suitable for practical applications such as automated systematic literature reviews and clinical decision support, and it suggests a general strategy for domain adaptation without retraining on full specialized corpora.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: GrowPage is a dynamic, on-demand KV-cache budgeting framework that adjusts KV capacity during decoding to improve the performance–throughput trade-off for long reasoning in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Long-output reasoning causes the KV cache to become a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Existing KV compression approaches assume a fixed per-request KV memory budget and only choose which KV entries to retain. This ignores that: (1) different requests inherently need different KV capacities; and (2) the attention patterns and thus KV needs of a single request change over the course of generation. There is a need for a mechanism that can adapt KV capacity on the fly to these heterogeneous and evolving demands, while remaining compatible with serving systems that use paging, continuous batching, and prefix caching.
AI.method: The paper proposes GrowPage, an on-demand KV budgeting framework. GrowPage models KV cache capacity as a runtime, elastic resource rather than a fixed budget. It maintains dual-timescale summaries of queries to track both recent and long-term attention behavior. Using these summaries, it estimates the evolving attention working set of each request. When the decoding process reaches a capacity boundary, GrowPage decides between: (1) compressing KV states within the existing allocation, or (2) acquiring additional physical KV pages if there is evidence of growing attention demand. The design is integrated with PagedAttention’s page-level memory abstraction so that GrowPage operates at the level of memory pages and is compatible with continuous batching and prefix caching.
AI.result: On reasoning benchmarks and across multiple LLMs, GrowPage demonstrates better performance–throughput trade-offs than prior KV compression or budgeting schemes. It can reduce memory-related bottlenecks and improve utilization without sacrificing, and sometimes improving, model accuracy and latency, outperforming baselines that rely on static per-request KV budgets.
AI.conclusion: Treating KV cache capacity as an elastic runtime resource, guided by dual-timescale attention summaries, allows more efficient and adaptive memory management for long reasoning tasks in LLMs. GrowPage, built on top of a page-based KV abstraction, delivers superior efficiency and scalability for LLM serving compared to fixed-budget KV compression approaches while remaining compatible with practical serving optimizations like continuous batching and prefix caching.

title: Contamination Inflates Scores but Rarely Reorders Large Language Model Leaderboards
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/DoriaXiao/anchor-dif
summary: Benchmark contamination, the leakage of test items into training data, is widely described as a threat to the reliability of large language model (LLM) leaderboards. We argue that this concern conflates two distinct questions: whether contamination inflates absolute scores, and whether it reorders the ranking of models. We recast contamination as a violation of anchor-item invariance and measure it through the differential functioning of original versus semantically equivalent paraphrased items, a within-item contrast that holds the measured skill fixed and isolates memorization from capability. Using per-instance responses from 47 publicly released models and 74 models finetuned with a known dose of contamination, across four benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU), we first calibrate the measure against ground truth: it recovers injected contamination dose-responsively (a corrected effect of +0.187 accuracy points for test-set leakage) and never flags a negative-control model trained only on the legitimate training split (-0.012). We then quantify leaderboard impact: the rank correlation between a standard leaderboard and a paraphrase-controlled leaderboard is 0.997, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the observed differential contamination is far below the level needed to move rankings, with only 3 of 188 model-by-benchmark cases showing differential contamination corroborated across two references. Contamination among these public models is therefore largely uniform: it inflates absolute scores without reordering the leaderboard, and ranking distortion requires the rare case of differential contamination. We provide a calibrated invariance audit, released as a reference implementation, and recommend that leaderboards report paraphrase-controlled rankings alongside confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates a method to detect and quantify benchmark contamination in LLMs using paraphrased test items, finding that while contamination inflates absolute scores, it rarely changes model rankings.
AI.motivation: Benchmark contamination is widely seen as undermining the credibility of LLM leaderboards, but discussion usually fails to distinguish between inflating absolute performance levels and distorting rankings. The authors aim to disentangle these effects and provide a rigorous, quantitative way to assess contamination that does not rely on access to training data or speculative data forensics.
AI.method: They recast contamination as a violation of anchor-item invariance, operationalized as differential performance on original test items versus semantically equivalent paraphrased versions. Using per-item responses from 47 public LLMs and 74 models finetuned with controlled contamination on four standard benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU), they (1) calibrate their measure by injecting known contamination levels and checking dose-response, and (2) construct “paraphrase-controlled” leaderboards where rankings are based on items whose behavior suggests little or no contamination. They also conduct sensitivity analyses to estimate how much differential contamination would be needed to reorder rankings.
AI.result: The contamination measure correctly tracks injected leakage, showing a positive, dose-responsive boost in accuracy (~+0.187 points for test-set leakage) and no signal for a negative-control model trained only on the benchmark’s training split (-0.012). When applying the method to 47 public models across four benchmarks, the rank correlation between standard and paraphrase-controlled leaderboards is extremely high (0.997), indicating almost identical rankings. Only 3 of 188 model–benchmark combinations show robust evidence of differential contamination across two independent paraphrase references.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark contamination in publicly released LLMs appears to be largely uniform across models: it systematically inflates absolute scores but almost never alters relative rankings. Distortion of leaderboards requires rare, model-specific differential contamination. The authors release a calibrated “invariance audit” implementation and recommend that future leaderboards report paraphrase-controlled rankings with confidence intervals to transparently account for contamination effects.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: They design a new DAG task scheduling algorithm for heterogeneous cloud–edge–end systems using PPO and spatio-temporal GNNs to improve load balancing and completion time.
AI.motivation: IoT drives many computation-intensive DAG applications that must run across heterogeneous cloud, edge, and end devices. Because these nodes differ in compute, bandwidth, and energy, and tasks have complex dependencies, efficient scheduling is NP-hard. Existing heuristics and standard RL methods cannot effectively model the spatio-temporal dynamics of resources, leading to suboptimal scheduling in dynamic heterogeneous environments.
AI.method: They propose PPO-STGNN, which combines proximal policy optimization (a policy-gradient RL algorithm) with a spatio-temporal graph neural network. The STGNN jointly encodes (1) the DAG task structure and (2) the physical cloud–edge–end resource graph, capturing both spatial relations and temporal evolution of resource states. PPO then learns a scheduling policy that maps these graph-based representations to task placement decisions. Additionally, they introduce a multi-teacher behavior-cloning pretraining stage, where the policy network is initialized by imitating multiple heuristic/teacher schedules to speed up convergence.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that PPO-STGNN significantly improves CPU and memory load balancing while keeping makespan and schedule length ratio low, i.e., it reduces resource hotspots without sacrificing overall completion time versus baselines.
AI.conclusion: Integrating STGNNs with PPO and multi-teacher behavior cloning yields a powerful scheduler for cloud–edge–end DAG workloads. It effectively captures spatio-temporal resource dynamics, achieves better load balancing, and maintains low completion time, making it well-suited for dynamic and heterogeneous DAG scheduling scenarios in IoT-style environments.

title: Dual-Form ASR: Semantics-Aware Inverse Text Normalization for Chinese Speech Recognition
summary: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) scenarios require both spoken-form transcripts for faithful transcription and readable written-form transcripts with inverse text normalization (ITN). However, these forms are typically produced by cascaded modules, where a spoken-form ASR output is rewritten by a separate ITN component, making written-form ASR-ITN vulnerable to recognition errors and decoupling normalization from acoustic-contextual modeling, especially for semantically dependent numeric expressions. In this paper, we propose Dual-Form ASR (DF-ASR), a framework that extends spoken-form ASR capability to semantics-aware written-form ITN through paired spoken-form and written-form supervision while retaining prompt-level selection between transcript forms. The dual-form supervision is constructed via a large language model (LLM)-driven generate-and-judge workflow, and training is further enhanced by ITN-MWER, a sequence-level objective that assigns higher cost to errors on normalization-sensitive spans. We also introduce a decision-aware REQUIRE-ITN/\FORBID-ITN protocol to separately measure required normalization and forbidden-span preservation. On manually annotated Chinese subsets from SpeechIO, DF-ASR consistently outperforms open-source ASR-ITN systems, remains competitive with strong closed-source references, and preserves reliable prompt-level control between spoken-form and written-form outputs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Dual-Form ASR (DF-ASR), an automatic speech recognition framework that jointly learns spoken-form and written-form (ITN) transcripts, improving normalization accuracy and controllability compared to cascaded ASR+ITN systems.
AI.motivation: Conventional ASR pipelines produce spoken-form transcripts that are later converted to human-readable written form via a separate inverse text normalization (ITN) module. This cascade is brittle: recognition errors propagate into ITN, and the normalization process cannot leverage acoustic or semantic context, which is particularly harmful for semantically dependent numeric expressions. The authors aim to tightly integrate recognition and normalization to make ASR both more accurate and more controllable in terms of output form.
AI.method: They introduce DF-ASR, which extends a spoken-form recognizer to also produce semantics-aware written-form outputs using paired supervision: each utterance is annotated with both spoken-form and written-form transcripts. These pairs are automatically created via an LLM-based generate-and-judge workflow. Training is further improved by ITN-MWER, a sequence-level loss that increases penalties on errors affecting normalization-sensitive spans (e.g., numbers, dates). The system allows prompt-level control between spoken-form and written-form outputs. They also propose a REQUIRE-ITN/FORBID-ITN evaluation protocol that separately measures performance on spans that must be normalized versus spans that must be preserved in spoken form.
AI.result: On manually annotated Chinese subsets from the SpeechIO dataset, DF-ASR consistently outperforms strong open-source ASR+ITN baselines and is competitive with closed-source commercial systems. It also provides reliable prompt-level control to switch between spoken and written forms without sacrificing recognition quality.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling ASR and ITN within a unified DF-ASR framework yields more accurate and robust written-form transcripts, especially on normalization-sensitive regions like numeric expressions, than traditional cascaded approaches. The proposed ITN-MWER objective and REQUIRE-ITN/FORBID-ITN evaluation protocol further improve and more precisely assess the handling of normalization versus preservation spans. The approach demonstrates strong performance on Chinese speech and maintains flexible control over transcript form.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how temporal aggregation methods for token importance scores affect KV cache compression at decoding time, showing that exponential moving average (EMA) aggregation makes many different scoring variants behave similarly, and proposes InertiaKV and Score-Free decoding as efficient, high-throughput approaches with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Existing work on decoding-time KV cache compression mainly focuses on designing better token scoring functions to decide which tokens to retain, but pays little attention to how scores are aggregated over time across decode steps. The authors suspect that this temporal aggregation rule might strongly influence which tokens are ultimately evicted or retained, especially under aggressive compression, and could overshadow differences between scoring functions while affecting model quality and throughput.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze various token scoring functions (e.g., value-norm, entropy, KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer) under aggressive KV compression, and compare them when combined with an exponential-moving-average (EMA) temporal aggregation rule. They measure how well these scorers preserve attention patterns and retention sets and how they affect ranking stability and model performance. Based on their findings, they design InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, which refreshes scores only periodically to reduce computation. They also evaluate a "Score-Free decoding" regime where scores are computed only once at the first step and then frozen, eliminating per-step scoring. Experiments are conducted on six open-weight LLM backbones over LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks.
AI.result: They find that with EMA aggregation, scoring functions that are approximately order-preserving with respect to attention (e.g., value-norm and entropy variants) produce highly correlated scores and nearly identical token retention sets, even under aggressive compression. Other scorers (KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer) modify token rankings more and lead to substantial degradation in performance. The analysis shows that the temporal aggregation rule couples layer weighting and temporal retention, making aggregation and ranking preservation key design factors. InertiaKV and InertiaKV-Lazy achieve 1.34–1.46x higher decoding throughput than a full-refresh InertiaKV baseline, while Score-Free decoding—scoring once and freezing the ranking—achieves nearly unchanged or slightly improved average quality (+0.03) with no subsequent scoring cost.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation strategy is a critical and distinct component in decoding-time KV cache compression, separate from the intrinsic quality of the scoring function. EMA-based aggregation can make many scoring variants effectively equivalent at the eviction level if they preserve relative ranking, while rank-altering scorers can harm performance. The proposed InertiaKV and InertiaKV-Lazy methods, along with the Score-Free decoding setting, demonstrate that carefully designed temporal aggregation and ranking preservation enable significant decoding throughput gains with negligible or even slightly positive impact on model quality, without suggesting that scoring quality itself is unimportant in all regimes.

title: RL-ADA: A World-Feedback Framework for Adversarially Robust Enterprise Dialogue Agents
summary: Deploying task-oriented dialogue agents in enterprise customer support faces a persistent annotation bottleneck: robust training requires labelled interaction data at scale, yet enterprise conversational logs are privacy-sensitive and expensive to annotate, while user behaviour evolves faster than labelling pipelines can keep pace. We present RL-ADA (Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Dialogue Agents), a co-evolutionary training framework that eliminates this bottleneck by replacing human labels with \emph{world feedback}: consequence-based reward signals derived directly from measurable interaction outcomes. A Customer Support Agent (DA, 3B parameters) and an Adversarial Customer Agent (CA, 7B parameters) co-evolve in an adversarial arena guided by a fixed automated judge: the DA is rewarded for correctly handling multi-turn customer conversations to successful resolution, while the CA is rewarded for producing realistic, intent-concealing utterances that cause misroutes, creating asymmetric adversarial pressure through opposing but independently structured rewards. An isolation gym iteratively retrains the weaker agent on prior-failure transcripts, requiring no human annotation at any stage. In a banking customer support proof of concept, tool-routing errors are eliminated and the strict end-to-end PASS rate doubles over five co-evolutionary cycles, driven solely by automated arena reward with no labelled data. We additionally observe the emergence of \textbf{Contextual Camouflage}, an adversarial strategy in which the CA learns to embed intent within dense realistic customer detail purely from reward pressure, with direct implications for enterprise red-teaming and robustness evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RL-ADA, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework where a dialogue agent and an adversarial customer agent train against each other using outcome-based rewards instead of human-labelled data, significantly improving task success in enterprise customer support.
AI.motivation: Enterprise task-oriented dialogue systems need large amounts of labelled interaction data, but obtaining such data is difficult because logs are privacy-sensitive, labels are expensive, and user behavior changes faster than annotation pipelines can adapt. The authors want to remove this annotation bottleneck while still improving robustness and performance of customer support agents in realistic, evolving settings.
AI.method: They introduce RL-ADA, where two large language model agents co-evolve: a Customer Support Agent (DA, 3B parameters) and an Adversarial Customer Agent (CA, 7B parameters). Both interact in an adversarial arena overseen by an automated judge that provides consequence-based rewards based on interaction outcomes instead of explicit labels. The DA is rewarded for accurately resolving multi-turn customer issues; the CA is rewarded for generating realistic, intent-hiding utterances that lead to misrouting and failures. An isolation gym then retrains the weaker agent on transcripts where it previously failed, iterating this process over multiple co-evolution cycles with no human annotation.
AI.result: In a banking customer support proof-of-concept, the system eliminates tool-routing errors and doubles the strict end-to-end PASS rate across five co-evolutionary cycles, all driven solely by automated arena rewards. The adversarial CA also develops a strategy termed "Contextual Camouflage," where it hides true intent within dense but realistic customer details, effectively stress-testing the DA.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-based, label-free co-evolution between a support agent and an adversarial customer simulator can substantially improve robustness and task success of enterprise dialogue systems, removing the need for manual annotation. The emergent adversarial behaviors like Contextual Camouflage highlight the value of such frameworks for red-teaming and robustness evaluation in real-world customer support applications.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CulturalMenuBench to test whether multimodal language models truly understand cultural aspects of food rather than just performing visual pattern matching.
AI.motivation: Despite high scores on existing food recognition benchmarks, it is unclear if multimodal models genuinely capture cultural and procedural knowledge about food or simply recognize visual appearances. The authors want to separate visual recognition ability from the capacity to apply cultural and procedural knowledge, especially around regional cuisines.
AI.method: They build CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions, with 10 tasks that combine final-dish and step-by-step cooking images, ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. The tasks range from simple recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. They then evaluate 12 multimodal language models on these tasks, perform diagnostic analyses of accuracy and error patterns, compare performance using images vs dish names, and run an ablation removing sequential images to test the role of procedural visual evidence.
AI.result: Models that achieve over 94% on standard multiple-choice food recognition tasks drop to at most 56% accuracy when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines with the same four-way multiple-choice setup. Errors look like random guessing, performance correlates more with how visually distinctive dishes are than with true cultural structure, and models are better at classifying cuisines from dish names alone than from images, with a 7–18 point accuracy gain. The ablation shows that removing sequential cooking images specifically harms process-grounded tasks while leaving others mostly unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark reveals a large gap between recognition and cultural knowledge application: models store relevant cultural knowledge but fail to access it from visual evidence, especially for process-grounded and regional-cuisine tasks. Near-perfect visual recognition hides this limitation. CulturalMenuBench thus motivates training approaches that explicitly link visual perception, procedural information, and cultural context, and it is released publicly to encourage further research.

title: Listen to the Latents: Self-Correcting Speech Recognition in Large Audio Language Models Through Hidden-State Interactions
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Recent automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems increasingly integrate large language models (LLMs) to leverage their semantic knowledge, either externally through logit fusion or internally through warm initialization. However, how to effectively combine these two strategies remains underexplored. In this work, we refine warm-initialized LLM-based ASR models by leveraging their own pre-adaptation base LLMs, focusing on LoRA-adapted settings where the base LLM is preserved. To achieve this, we propose Hybrid Search, a targeted correction strategy motivated by two observations. First, interaction features that characterize the relationship between LLM-based ASR hidden states and base-LLM hidden states provide informative signals about a token's degree of semantic dependence. Second, selectively refining targeted tokens with high semantic dependence improves ASR performance far beyond naive global LLM-correction methods including rescoring and late fusion. Our analysis suggests that, even after semantic knowledge transfer through warm initialization, LLM-based ASR models can still leverage their base LLM to further improve inference-time performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Hybrid Search, a method that uses interaction between an ASR-adapted LLM and its original base LLM to selectively correct high-semantic-dependence tokens, significantly improving ASR over standard LLM-based correction and fusion methods.
AI.motivation: Modern ASR systems increasingly use LLMs both as external language models (logit fusion, rescoring) and as internal components via warm initialization, but the best way to combine these two paradigms is unclear. Even after adaptation for ASR, the base LLM’s rich semantic knowledge may remain underused. The authors want to understand whether, and how, the original base LLM can still help the adapted ASR-LLM at inference time, in a way that is more effective than simple global rescoring or fusion.
AI.method: They study LoRA-adapted LLM-based ASR models where the base LLM weights are preserved. They define interaction features between the hidden states of the ASR-LLM and the untouched base LLM to quantify each token’s semantic dependence. Based on these features, they introduce Hybrid Search: a targeted correction strategy that, during decoding, selectively invokes the base LLM to refine only those tokens identified as having high semantic dependence, instead of applying global correction to all tokens. They compare this targeted approach against naive global LLM correction strategies such as rescoring and late fusion.
AI.result: The proposed interaction features reliably indicate which tokens are highly dependent on semantic context. Using these features to drive Hybrid Search, the system selectively refines only those critical tokens and achieves ASR performance substantially better than naive global LLM-correction methods, including rescoring and late fusion baselines. This demonstrates that the base LLM still provides useful complementary information even after warm initialization and LoRA adaptation for ASR.
AI.conclusion: Warm-initialized, LoRA-adapted LLM-based ASR models do not fully subsume the semantic knowledge of their base LLMs; the base models remain valuable at inference time. By modeling interactions between the adapted ASR-LLM and its base LLM and using them to target semantically dependent tokens, the Hybrid Search strategy yields superior ASR performance compared to global correction methods. This shows that carefully combining internal adaptation with external LLM use can meaningfully enhance ASR quality.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NeoRed, a multimodal large language model specifically designed for neonatal respiratory disease report generation, overcoming domain gaps and improving multimodal clinical reasoning via a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment framework, and showing superior performance over existing MLLMs on new neonatal datasets.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in newborns, yet current multimodal LLMs for medical imaging are mostly trained on adult data and fail to fully exploit rich, multidimensional neonatal clinical context. This creates a domain gap and leads to suboptimal diagnostic report generation in neonatal settings. The authors aim to build a model and datasets tailored to neonatal respiratory disease to improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical usefulness of generated reports.
AI.method: The authors collect two real-world neonatal clinical datasets, NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV, comprising chest X-rays and associated clinical information. They propose NeoRed, a specialized multimodal large language model for neonatal respiratory diseases, built around a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework. KLA constrains report generation via three components: (1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI), which injects neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations to focus attention on disease-relevant patterns; (2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC), which aligns the semantics of generated text with a coherent multimodal diagnostic reasoning process; and (3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA), which aligns visual features from CXRs with textual imaging conclusions to ensure consistency between image evidence and narrative findings.
AI.result: On the NeoCXR dataset, NeoRed achieves a ROUGE-L score of 53.29% and a Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19%, outperforming existing general-purpose MLLMs on neonatal report generation. It also maintains competitive performance on adult chest X-ray benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray), indicating that specialization for neonates does not sacrifice broader applicability.
AI.conclusion: NeoRed is, to the authors’ knowledge, the first multimodal LLM specialized for neonatal respiratory disease report generation, effectively addressing domain gap and context-integration limitations in prior models. The proposed Knowledge-Logic-Alignment framework improves alignment between medical knowledge, diagnostic reasoning, and visual evidence, leading to more accurate and clinically effective neonatal diagnostic reports. The newly introduced NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV datasets provide valuable benchmarks for future research and will be available upon application.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge: Concerning Rubric Artifacts in LLM-based Automated Text Generation Evaluation
comment: Accepted for publication at EMNLP 2026. 5 pages, 6 figures
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are increasingly used to evaluate AI-generated text, based on the assumption that judgments arise from reasoning over candidate responses with respect to a rubric. We show that this assumption warrants further scrutiny. Classifiers trained only on rubric text, without access to any evaluated response, achieve nontrivial predictive performance on judge outputs. This suggests that rubric formulations encode recoverable evaluative signals, allowing scores to be partially anticipated independently of model outputs. Finally, counterfactual perturbations reveal that judges often fail to reliably update their decisions when either the candidate response or the rubric criterion is reversed. Our findings raise concerns about the reliability of rubric-based LLM evaluation and highlight the need for further methodological study of automated evaluation via LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper questions the reliability of using LLMs as automatic judges by showing that rubric wording alone can predict evaluation scores and that judges often ignore key changes in responses or rubrics.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to automatically evaluate AI-generated text, under the assumption that they carefully compare responses against detailed rubrics. However, this practice is becoming widespread without much validation of how reliable or faithful these rubric-based evaluations actually are. The authors aim to test whether LLM judges truly reason over both rubric and response, or whether evaluations are partially determined by superficial properties of the rubric itself.
AI.method: The authors train classifiers that receive only the evaluation rubric text—without seeing any candidate response—to predict the scores that LLM judges assign. They then measure how well these classifiers approximate the real judge outputs. Additionally, they perform counterfactual perturbation experiments where they reverse or alter either (a) the candidate response or (b) specific rubric criteria, and test whether LLM judges correspondingly change their scores. This probes how sensitive and faithful LLM judges are to the actual content of the rubric and responses.
AI.result: Classifiers that see only the rubric (no candidate answers) achieve nontrivial accuracy in predicting LLM-judge scores, indicating that the rubric wording itself carries strong, exploitable signals about the expected evaluation outcome. In the counterfactual experiments, LLM judges frequently fail to adjust their scores appropriately when key aspects of the response or rubric are reversed, revealing a lack of robust, criterion-based reasoning. These effects persist across multiple settings, suggesting systematic weaknesses rather than isolated failures.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current rubric-based LLM-as-a-Judge setups are less reliable than commonly assumed. Evaluations can be partly anticipated from rubric formulations alone, and judges do not always behave as faithful, criterion-following evaluators. This casts doubt on the validity of automated evaluation pipelines that rely on LLM judges and underscores the need for better methodology, more robust evaluation designs, and deeper analysis of how LLMs use rubrics when scoring model outputs.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FreNet, a lesion segmentation framework that reconfigures features using visual priors before and during encoding, achieving substantial performance gains over SOTA methods on multiple medical imaging benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Lesion segmentation in medical images is difficult due to complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder approaches mostly strengthen feature extraction or decoding, but they lack early prior guidance and explicit feature reconfiguration in the encoding stage, which limits their ability to suppress background noise and adapt to varied lesion shapes and appearances.
AI.method: The authors introduce FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework guided by visual priors. First, they design an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) that models a continuous spatial field and uses priors from SAM to reconfigure the input image at the pixel level before encoding, suppressing irrelevant background. Second, they propose a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module that operates during the encoding stage. DFR consists of a Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM), which decouples backbone features into frequency components to enhance foreground–background separability, and a Spatial Localization Module (SLM), which relocates and stabilizes spatial information after frequency processing. These components are integrated into an encoder-decoder segmentation network.
AI.result: FreNet is evaluated on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks spanning three imaging modalities. It consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods. On the particularly challenging ETIS dataset, FreNet improves Dice score by 5.0% over the previous SOTA method and by 7.2% over SAM, demonstrating strong robustness to background clutter and lesion variability.
AI.conclusion: Early, prior-guided feature reconfiguration and dual-domain (frequency and spatial) feature processing during encoding substantially improve lesion segmentation performance. By leveraging SAM-based visual priors through IPNN and refining backbone features with DFR, FreNet effectively suppresses background interference and handles diverse lesion morphologies, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.

title: LexIssue: Benchmarking Legal Issue Identification in Chinese Civil Litigation
summary: Identifying the issues disputed between litigating parties is a crucial component of real-world litigation. However, legal issues remain comparatively underexplored in legal AI research. In this work, we study the computational modelling of legal issue identification in litigation. We introduce a legally grounded hierarchical schema that represents legal issues through both free-form issue descriptions and structured legal categories, and formulate legal issue identification as two complementary tasks: legal issue generation and legal issue classification. Based on this formulation, we construct LexIssue, a benchmark containing 430 real-world Chinese civil litigation cases and 1,303 expert-annotated disputed legal issues. We further develop an issue-centric legal knowledge base spanning 27 causes of action and 441 candidate legal issue entries to support retrieval-augmented reasoning. Experimental results across a diverse set of models show that retrieval-augmented generation using the constructed legal issue knowledge base consistently improves performance in identifying disputed legal issues and their corresponding legal attributes.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a benchmark and method for automatically identifying disputed legal issues in Chinese civil litigation using a hierarchical schema and retrieval-augmented models.
AI.motivation: In real-world litigation, clearly identifying what specific legal issues are actually in dispute between parties is essential, but existing legal AI focuses more on tasks like judgment prediction or statute retrieval, leaving issue identification underexplored. This gap limits the practical usefulness of legal AI systems in assisting real case workflows.
AI.method: The authors design a hierarchical schema that encodes disputed legal issues as both natural-language descriptions and structured legal categories. They formalize legal issue identification as two tasks: (1) legal issue generation (producing free-form issue descriptions) and (2) legal issue classification (mapping issues to predefined categories). They then build LexIssue, a dataset of 430 Chinese civil cases with 1,303 expert-annotated issues, and construct an issue-centric legal knowledge base covering 27 causes of action and 441 typical issues. Finally, they test various models, including retrieval-augmented generation that leverages the knowledge base to better identify issues and their attributes.
AI.result: The LexIssue benchmark and the associated knowledge base are successfully constructed. Experiments with a variety of models demonstrate that using retrieval-augmented generation with the issue knowledge base consistently yields better performance in both generating and classifying disputed legal issues than baselines without retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Legal issue identification in litigation can be effectively modeled as joint generation and classification over a hierarchical, legally grounded schema. A dedicated benchmark (LexIssue) and an issue-centric knowledge base enable more realistic evaluation and significantly improve performance via retrieval-augmented approaches, advancing the development of practical legal AI tools for litigation support.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dalek, a closed, self-maintaining, self-evolving agent machine based on actors, messages, and channels, capable of operating on any substrate that meets a general host contract.
AI.motivation: To build a general, substrate-independent machine for agents that can internally realize and close the loop on self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization, extending von Neumann’s ideas to modern text-and-message-based AI systems.
AI.method: Define a minimal set of structural primitives (actors, messages, channels) plus four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity), and integrate von Neumann’s self-reproducing automaton core with a text-and-message substrate. Implement Dalek such that a large language model and a compiler occupy a payload slot, enabling the system to author, compile, install, and inherit new capabilities and internal components.
AI.result: A concrete machine design (Dalek) that structurally enforces closure of boundary, identity, heredity, and evolution for agent systems. Dalek demonstrates how an LLM+compiler payload can serve as a general capability producer, generating both functional capabilities and the machine’s own organs and runtime, with these changes inherited by descendants.
AI.conclusion: Dalek provides a principled architecture for self-maintaining, self-evolving agent machines on a general host substrate, rederiving and extending von Neumann’s self-reproducing automaton to modern agentic AI. By structurally closing heredity and evolution within the machine via its construction language and obligations, Dalek offers a path toward robust, self-organizing artificial agents with explicit boundaries and identities.

title: Unifying Conformal Language Tasks with In-Context Ensembles
comment: Findings of EMNLP 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/conformal-relevance
summary: Many NLP tasks, such as summarization and extractive question answering, reduce to retrieving relevant content from documents under two constraints: coverage, retaining enough pertinent information to achieve some goal, and conciseness, removing as much irrelevant information as possible. Conformal prediction methods have been used to guarantee coverage, and must be optimized for conciseness through design of a score function. State-of-the-art scoring functions use hand-engineered LLM prompts asking the model to rate the importance of content, but manual prompt engineering is labor-intensive and task-specific. We introduce the Conformal Relevance framework which uses in-context learning example curation and ensembling to create a score function which maintains coverage while improving conciseness with minimal manual input. We demonstrate this framework's application on seven NLP tasks, and also theoretically study the impact of diversity for ensembled conformal scores, giving a complementarity condition that characterizes when ensembling improves worst-case sentence scores, and a saturation bound on ensemble improvement.

AI.tldr: A framework called Conformal Relevance automatically builds conformal prediction-based scoring functions for NLP retrieval tasks, improving conciseness while preserving coverage, using in-context learning and ensembling instead of manual LLM prompt engineering.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP retrieval tasks like summarization and extractive QA require both coverage of relevant info and conciseness, but conformal prediction methods, while good at coverage guarantees, rely on hand-engineered, task-specific LLM prompts to define score functions, which is labor-intensive and not scalable.
AI.method: They propose the Conformal Relevance framework that: (1) uses in-context learning with curated examples to teach LLMs to rate content importance; (2) constructs conformal score functions from these ratings; and (3) ensembles multiple such scores to balance coverage and conciseness. They also theoretically analyze how diversity between conformal scores affects ensemble performance, deriving a complementarity condition and a saturation bound on ensemble improvement.
AI.result: Applied across seven NLP tasks, the framework maintains the formal coverage guarantees of conformal prediction while empirically yielding more concise retrieved content than manually engineered scoring baselines. Theoretical results characterize when and how much ensembling diverse conformal scores can improve worst-case sentence-level scores.
AI.conclusion: Conformal Relevance reduces manual prompt engineering by automating the construction of conformal score functions via in-context learning and ensembling, preserving coverage guarantees while improving conciseness across multiple NLP tasks, and providing theoretical insight into the benefits and limits of ensemble diversity for conformal prediction.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: Introduces GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark to evaluate LLM-based governance policy simulations using real-world records and structured actor modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based policy simulations can produce plausible narratives but lack validated grounding in real-world evidence and actors, making it unclear whether they are actually useful for policy analysis beyond toy examples or hypothetical scenarios. There is no standard empirical setting to rigorously test whether multi-agent simulations or different reasoning schemes genuinely improve prediction and understanding of policy outcomes. The authors aim to bridge this gap by building a benchmark that anchors simulations in documented legislative, lobbying, regulatory, and economic data, enabling systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The authors construct GPS-Bench, a benchmark that links specific policies to concrete actors, their actions, and downstream impacts using diverse public data sources (legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data, etc.). Actors (personas) are reconstructed from time-stamped records with provenance rather than generic archetypes, turning them into evidence objects. They create a Gold evaluation set via human annotation and a Silver supervision set via a separate LLM using retrieved evidence, ensuring Silver labels are never used as test labels. The benchmark defines a common grounded state and uniform output schema across inference modes. They then systematically compare multiple modeling approaches over the same policy state: single joint reasoning, independent actors, communicating actor agents, graph-based methods, and weight-level fine-tuning on the grounded record, with agents sometimes holding private, non-identical evidence and engaging in explicit proposal and coalition-formation dialogues.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on the grounded record yields the strongest performance for predicting actor-level impacts of policies. Decomposed multi-agent setups (independent or communicating agents, graph-based methods, etc.) do not surpass this fine-tuned baseline in predictive accuracy. However, multi-agent decomposition contributes richer mechanism-level explanations: agents use their private evidence, refer to specific exposure clauses, and negotiate with named partners through concrete proposals, trade-offs, and justifications. This structure allows the resulting coalitions to be empirically checked against the commitments documented in the historical record.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench provides a unified, evidence-grounded environment for evaluating LLM-based governance policy simulations, focusing on real actors and documented impacts. While fine-tuning on grounded records is most effective for predicting actor outcomes, multi-agent decomposition mainly adds interpretability and mechanistic insight rather than raw accuracy gains. The benchmark enables controlled comparisons of evidence use, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction, supporting future research on when and how these components improve the prediction and explanation of policy outcomes.

title: SHELF: A Synthetic Harness for Multi-Task Bibliographic Benchmarking
comment: 17 pages, 15 tables. Code available at https://github.com/mjbommar/shelf-benchmark ; data available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mjbommar/SHELF
summary: Libraries and archives manage large collections with limited staff and computing budgets, yet common benchmarks do not systematically test their bibliographic work. They need to know which methods work for their tasks and what those methods require to run. SHELF, the Synthetic Harness for Evaluating LLM Fitness, addresses this gap. It is a Python system that turns labelled taxonomies, writing specifications, and a generation budget into controlled benchmark data and evaluation tasks. This first release contains 62,899 model-written documents based on Library of Congress vocabularies, with tasks for classification, clustering, retrieval, pair classification, and instruction retrieval. We compare TF, TF-IDF, BM25, popular encoders, and, on subject classification only, zero-shot decoders; each method appears only on tasks that support it. Subject classification reaches 0.8887, while genre-form classification reaches only 0.2605, and several pair and clustering tasks remain near chance. Sparse methods remain competitive on classification, while TF-IDF is the fastest measured arm in the subject timing experiment. SHELF also varies bibliographic facets independently and can generate new, verifiably unseen documents after a model's training cutoff. Comparisons with LCSHBench and Project Gutenberg show that model rankings transfer more reliably than absolute scores, but SHELF scores do not estimate accuracy on production catalogue data. We release all source code and data under permissive licenses on GitHub and Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: Introduces SHELF, a Python-based synthetic benchmarking system using library taxonomies to evaluate LLM and IR methods on realistic bibliographic tasks under resource constraints.
AI.motivation: Libraries and archives have large, complex bibliographic collections but limited staff and compute, and existing benchmarks do not align with or systematically test their real cataloging and retrieval tasks. Practitioners need to know which NLP/LLM and IR methods are effective and affordable for domain-specific tasks such as subject and genre classification, clustering, and retrieval, and how these methods behave on data that reflects real bibliographic structures.
AI.method: The authors build SHELF (Synthetic Harness for Evaluating LLM Fitness), a Python framework that uses labeled taxonomies (e.g., Library of Congress vocabularies), writing specifications, and a generation budget to synthesize controlled benchmark datasets and evaluation tasks. The first release includes 62,899 LLM-generated documents conditioned on Library of Congress subject and genre vocabularies. They define multiple tasks: classification (subject, genre-form), clustering, retrieval, pair classification, and instruction retrieval. They benchmark several baselines: sparse text representations (TF, TF-IDF, BM25), dense encoders, and zero-shot decoders (for subject classification only). They also measure runtime and explore how varying bibliographic facets and generating post-cutoff documents impact evaluation. They compare model rankings and scores across SHELF, LCSHBench, and Project Gutenberg corpora to study transferability to other datasets and production-like settings.
AI.result: SHELF produces a large synthetic benchmark (62,899 documents) with multiple bibliographic tasks. On subject classification, the best models reach high accuracy (0.8887), but performance on genre-form classification is much lower (0.2605), and some pair and clustering tasks hover near chance, indicating substantial task difficulty. Sparse methods (TF, TF-IDF, BM25) remain competitive with dense encoders on classification, and TF-IDF is the fastest method in subject classification timing experiments. The framework can independently vary bibliographic facets and generate documents that are guaranteed unseen after an LLM's training cutoff. Cross-corpus comparisons show that while absolute performance scores do not transfer well to production catalog data, relative model rankings are more stable across SHELF, LCSHBench, and Project Gutenberg benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SHELF fills an evaluation gap for libraries and archives by offering a reproducible, synthetic, and controllable benchmarking framework tailored to bibliographic tasks and resource constraints. It demonstrates that simple sparse methods can still perform strongly and efficiently, that some bibliographic tasks—especially genre-form categorization and certain pair/clustering setups—are inherently challenging, and that synthetic benchmarks can meaningfully reflect relative model rankings even if they do not directly predict real-world accuracy. The open-source release on GitHub and Hugging Face provides practitioners and researchers with a practical tool for testing and comparing methods for cataloging and retrieval in library contexts.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

AI.tldr: They build HalluPeer, a benchmark to detect hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, showing existing detectors often fail and that these hallucination patterns appear in real reviews.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to assist academic peer review but often generate fluent yet unsupported claims (hallucinations), especially problematic because verification must be grounded in long, technical papers. Existing hallucination benchmarks don't match this peer-review setting, so there is no suitable way to evaluate or train systems for reliable, source-grounded review assistance.
AI.method: They construct HalluPeer, a benchmark consisting of aligned triples: (1) scientific paper content, (2) original human-written reviews, and (3) hallucination-injected versions of those reviews. They design a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identify relevant review contexts, automatically inject hallucinations into reviews, and filter them. The dataset is annotated for three tasks: hallucination detection (is there a hallucination?), classification (what type?), and localization (where is it?). They then run experiments using existing hallucination detectors on a large collection of papers and reviews to assess performance.
AI.result: On 12K papers and 38K reviews, existing hallucination detectors perform poorly at distinguishing hallucinations from valid critical comments in reviews. When applied to real (authentic) peer reviews, the patterns of hallucinations formalized in HalluPeer are indeed observed, confirming that such hallucinations are not only synthetic artifacts but occur in practice.
AI.conclusion: HalluPeer provides a peer-review-specific benchmark and taxonomy for hallucination detection, showing that current detectors are not yet adequate for the nuanced setting of scientific peer review. The occurrence of HalluPeer-style hallucinations in real reviews underscores the need for source-aware verification methods when using LLMs as peer-review assistants.

title: Large Language Models in Resolving Contextual Knowledge Conflicts
summary: Most prior works focused on conflicts between an LLM's internal parametric knowledge and externally provided context. In contrast, we investigate how LLMs handle conflicts that arise within contextual knowledge itself. We introduce a taxonomy of six types of contextual conflicts (factual, inferential, temporal, granularity, perspective, and ambiguity) and contribute a comprehensive dataset ContextConflict for this setting. The dataset contains 5,781 samples, covers both reasoning and summarization tasks, and includes both explicit contradictions and implicit conflicts that require multi-step reasoning. Experiments on nine LLMs show that current models still fall short in resolving contextual knowledge conflicts. We further provide mechanistic interpretability insights into how LLMs process such conflicts, revealing their latent awareness of conflicts and the representational geometry underlying conflict processing. In addition, our analysis uncovers a consistent model bias towards earlier evidence, and this positional preference serves as a key obstacle to effective conflict resolution. Motivated by these findings, we further propose a simple training-free, label-free steering method that steers activations to encourage a more comprehensive incorporation of evidences for better conflict resolution. On our dataset, the method consistently improves accuracy on reasoning tasks and generates higher-quality, more balanced summaries for summarization tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models handle conflicts within the given context itself, builds a taxonomy and dataset of such conflicts, analyzes model behavior and internal mechanisms, finds strong biases (especially toward early evidence), and proposes a simple inference-time steering method that improves conflict resolution without extra training or labels.
AI.motivation: Existing work mainly examines conflicts between a model’s internal knowledge and external context, but in real use, conflicts often exist within the provided context (multiple pieces of evidence disagreeing). There was no systematic taxonomy, dataset, or in-depth analysis of how LLMs handle these intra-context conflicts, nor practical methods to mitigate failure modes.
AI.method: 1) Define six types of contextual conflicts (factual, inferential, temporal, granularity, perspective, ambiguity). 2) Construct ContextConflict, a 5,781-sample dataset spanning reasoning and summarization tasks, containing both explicit contradictions and implicit multi-step conflicts. 3) Benchmark nine LLMs on this dataset. 4) Use mechanistic interpretability to study how conflicts are internally represented, detecting latent conflict awareness, representational geometry of conflict tokens, and positional biases. 5) Design a simple, training-free, label-free activation steering method at inference to reduce positional bias and encourage better integration of all evidences.
AI.result: LLMs significantly underperform on tasks requiring resolving conflicts within the context, across both reasoning and summarization. Mechanistic analyses show models internally register conflict signals and structure conflicting evidence in representation space but still default to a strong bias toward earlier evidence, harming performance. The proposed training-free activation steering consistently improves reasoning accuracy and leads to more balanced, higher-quality summaries on the ContextConflict benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Contextual conflict resolution is a distinct and unsolved challenge for LLMs, even when they appear to encode awareness of conflicts internally. A key obstacle is a stable positional bias toward early evidence. The new taxonomy and ContextConflict dataset provide a foundation for future study, and a simple, training-free steering approach demonstrates that better use of existing representations can significantly improve conflict handling without re-training or supervision.

title: The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models
summary: Audio-video diffusion models rely on cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, yet this same mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. We study these models by probing and analyzing the ``attention triangle,'' comprising the three cross-attention edges connecting the text, audio, and video streams, and examine how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation. Our analysis reveals that routing along the audio-video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation, while video can influence audio generation. This edge is shaped by biases encoded in the model's parameters and emerges as a major contributor to leakage: when prompts are in tension with learned priors, cross-modal interactions may override the intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. These effects suggest that semantic artifacts arise not merely from attention spreading beyond its intended target, but from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific pathways. Building on this perspective, we extract attention-derived signals that expose how semantics are distributed and grounded across modalities, and use them as a diagnostic tool to both analyze and deliberately incur leakage under controlled conditions. This enables us to probe the internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolate the role of individual interactions. We further leverage these signals to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments support our analysis and demonstrate improved semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes and controls semantic leakage in audio-video diffusion models caused by cross-modal attention between text, audio, and video, and proposes attention-based diagnostics and interventions to improve cross-modal semantic alignment without hurting quality.
AI.motivation: Audio-video diffusion models often generate outputs where text, audio, and video are not semantically consistent—for example, the visuals may contradict the sound or the prompt. This inconsistency is partly due to how cross-modal attention routes information across modalities, but the internal routing mechanisms and their failure modes are poorly understood. The authors aim to understand how semantic information flows between text, audio, and video, why it sometimes overrides the conditioning prompt, and how to systematically diagnose and mitigate these cross-modal semantic leakage issues.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize the model’s cross-modal attention as an “attention triangle” among text, audio, and video streams. They probe each cross-attention edge, with particular focus on the audio-video edge, to see how semantic information is routed during generation. They perform attention-based analyses to detect when semantics deviate from the prompt and are instead driven by model priors. From this, they derive attention-based signals that reveal how semantics are grounded across modalities. They then design controlled experiments to deliberately induce leakage using these signals, isolating the role of specific interactions. Finally, they use the extracted signals at inference time to implement interventions that steer attention patterns toward better cross-modal consistency.
AI.result: The analysis shows that the audio-video cross-attention edge is bidirectional: audio affects video generation and video affects audio generation. This edge encodes strong biases from the model’s parameters and is a primary pathway for semantic leakage, especially when the text prompt conflicts with the model’s learned priors. They demonstrate that leakage is not just diffuse attention but arises from structured, bias-driven routing along particular attention paths. Using the attention-derived signals as diagnostics, they can expose where and how semantics are misrouted, and can deliberately trigger or control leakage in experiments. The proposed inference-time interventions, guided by these signals, yield better semantic grounding and cross-modal alignment, while maintaining overall generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Semantic leakage in audio-video diffusion models stems from structured, biased cross-modal interactions, particularly along the audio-video attention edge, rather than from generic attention spillover. By modeling cross-modal attention as an attention triangle and extracting informative attention-derived signals, one can diagnose how semantics are routed and grounded across modalities, experimentally manipulate leakage, and design inference-time controls. These controls improve cross-modal semantic alignment between text, audio, and video without degrading output quality, offering a principled path toward more reliable multimodal generative models.

title: No country for old linguists: LLM-brain alignment underdetermines neural computation
summary: Nastase et al. (2026) argue that large language models (LLMs) may illuminate language processing because both rely on distributed, context-sensitive representations shaped by statistical learning. Their rejection of simple cortical "boxology" is persuasive, and they articulate a strong case for the value of LLM-brain alignment research. The key question is what kind of inference LLM-brain alignment licenses. My claim here will be narrow: representational alignment can in principle constrain mechanistic hypotheses, but it does not by itself identify a mechanism. Nastase et al. acknowledge that an encoding model can capture features represented in neural activity without establishing a shared architecture or algorithm. Yet the authors sometime move from alignment to "shared computational principles" and ultimately to LLMs as mechanistic models of natural language. Indeed, their methodological caveat that alignment does not establish a shared architecture or algorithm sits uneasily with their conclusion that LLMs might instantiate the same computational principles as biological brains and provide a "fully mechanistic model" of language. I discuss what I consider to be problems of logical, causal, and computational underdetermination in Nastase et al.'s (2026) proposal.
