This work suggests that effective personalization and safe assistance require not just instruction-following but also sophisticated, context-aware retrieval and reasoning over egocentric knowledge.

title: Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State
summary:
Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

AI.tldr: Transfiver is a framework for long-term human-AI interaction that keeps all interaction-specific information in a shared, editable state updated by both the model and the human.
AI.motivation: In long-term human-AI interaction, the model’s internal information that guides inference is implicitly updated and opaque to users, making it hard to inspect, control, or correct. The authors want a way for humans to directly see and edit the information that conditions future model behavior.
AI.method: They propose Transfiver, an architecture where all interaction-specific information is stored in a single persistent state S_t that is shared between the human and the model. The framework defines two kinds of updates to this state: (1) implicit stream updates, where the model automatically interprets the interaction and revises or adds state items; and (2) explicit directed edits, where the human inspects specific items and edits them directly. The architecture also separates fixed shared parameters θ, learned offline, from the persistent state S_t, which evolves during deployment without retraining parameters.
AI.result: Conceptually, Transfiver enables human and model to co-manage the same underlying state so that human corrections directly alter what subsequent computation reads, rather than being just additional instructions. The paper presents the framework and its design; extending it to more complex, large-scale natural-language and relational states is identified as future work.
AI.conclusion: Transfiver offers a principled way to make long-term human-AI interaction more transparent and controllable by maintaining a shared editable state that both humans and models can update, decoupled from static model parameters. However, realizing this approach for rich, large-scale real-world settings remains an open challenge.

title: Decoupling Turn-Taking from Semantics: A Decoupled Data Approach for Finite-State-Machine-Based Full-Duplex Dialogue
summary: The Neural Finite State Machine (NFSM) framework offers a pragmatic path to full-duplex dialogue by serializing turn-taking control and response generation onto a single causal tape under the standard next-token prediction objective, thereby preserving semantic prowess at a low fine-tuning cost. However, its reliance on synthetic text data fundamentally limits turn-taking naturalness, as Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot faithfully simulate the fine-grained acoustic temporal dynamics of real human dialogues. In this work, we propose a decoupled data approach that learns turn-taking from real Human-Human (HH) spoken dialogues while shaping semantic behavior through configurable Human-Agent (HA) text dialogues. To operationalize this approach, we introduce a rule-based event-guided data transformation method that serializes HH spoken dialogues into FSM tapes by classifying turn-taking events and applying deterministic mapping rules, enabling scalable supervision without LLM-generated annotations. We further propose a Source-Aware Calibrated (SAC) Loss that jointly calibrates the long-tailed distribution of state transition tokens and channels each data source toward the capability it best supervises. Experiments show that our approach substantially improves turn-taking proficiency while recovering the foundation LLM's semantic capability. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/Liyht/def-fsm.

AI.tldr: They improve NFSM-based full-duplex dialogue by learning turn-taking from real speech and semantics from configurable text, using rule-based serialization of human-human audio dialogues and a new loss to calibrate data sources and rare transition tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing Neural Finite State Machine (NFSM) methods for full-duplex dialogue serialize turn-taking and response generation on one token stream but depend on synthetic, LLM-generated dialogue data. Because LLMs cannot model fine-grained acoustic timing, this synthetic data leads to unnatural turn-taking, limiting real-world usability, even though fine-tuning cost is low and semantics are strong.
AI.method: 1) Propose a decoupled data strategy where turn-taking behavior is learned from real human-human spoken dialogues, while semantic and behavioral aspects are learned from configurable human-agent text dialogues. 2) Introduce a rule-based, event-guided data transformation that converts multi-modal HH spoken dialogues into FSM tapes, by detecting and classifying turn-taking events (e.g., holds, transfers, overlaps) and applying deterministic mapping rules—thus avoiding LLM annotation. 3) Design a Source-Aware Calibrated (SAC) Loss that (a) rebalances the long-tailed distribution of state-transition tokens in the FSM tape, and (b) differentially weights or calibrates losses from each data source (HH vs HA) so each source supervises the capabilities it best supports.
AI.result: Empirical experiments show that the proposed method significantly improves the model’s turn-taking behavior (e.g., more natural interruptions, less latency, fewer cut-offs) compared to the baseline NFSM trained on synthetic data, while also restoring or preserving the underlying LLM’s semantic competence, which was degraded in previous NFSM training regimes. The source-aware calibration and rule-based serialization both contribute clearly to these gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling turn-taking and semantic supervision across different data sources, combined with rule-based spoken-dialogue serialization and a source-aware calibrated loss, enables NFSM-based full-duplex dialogue systems that better match human conversational timing without sacrificing semantic quality. This offers a scalable, low-cost path toward more natural spoken agents and shows that NFSM-style token-level control can be effectively trained from real human speech logs without LLM-generated annotations.

title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
summary: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques federated learning as insufficient for preventing extractive AI and proposes governance principles that extend from data to models and their federation.
AI.motivation: Although federated learning is marketed as a privacy-preserving and fairer paradigm because data stays on user devices, the authors observe that it often leaves power and control over resulting models with central conveners, perpetuating extractive relationships with creators and contributors. They want to rethink federation from the standpoint of creative communities, focusing on who governs not only data but also models and learning practices.
AI.method: The authors conceptually decompose how creative communities can hold and govern their work into three layers: storage, circulation, and learning. They examine existing governance forms—artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures—to see where creator control is currently established and where it breaks down. Based on that analysis, they outline technical and human research problems and distill design principles for a new kind of creative data commons.
AI.result: They find that current creator and community governance mechanisms typically cover storage (where data lives) and circulation (how it is shared or licensed), but effectively stop at learning: contributors can consent or refuse their data being used for training, but they have almost no influence over how models are trained, how federated learning is organized, or how resulting models are used and governed. The analysis surfaces a space of intertwined technical and social research questions needed to address this gap.
AI.conclusion: Federation alone does not solve extractive AI; what matters is governance over both data and models, including their federation. The authors propose four design principles for a creative data commons that addresses this: (1) govern the model, not only the underlying corpus; (2) make governance terms understandable at the moment contributors share their work; (3) treat refusal and opting out as first-class, supported states; and (4) determine and practice stewardship in an open, accountable manner.

title: How Perturbations Propagate: A Multi-Level Analysis of Robustness in Large Language Models
summary: Language models encounter typos, corrupted text, altered words, and disrupted token order, yet robustness is usually evaluated only through output behavior. We study how six naturalistic and synthetic input perturbations propagate through decoder-only language models at three levels: output behavior, hidden-state geometry, and attention-head function. We evaluate behavioral effects across four GPT-2 and two Qwen2.5 checkpoints by analyzing layerwise geometry using centered kernel alignment and intrinsic dimension, and examine attention-head responses in GPT-2. Perturbation types produce distinguishable metric profiles that are not fully captured by output measures and are only partly consistent across the tested checkpoints. Copying scores are especially associated with activation-patching recovery under token substitution and shuffling. Gradient-guided HotFlip perturbations also cause stronger behavioral and representational disruption than rate-matched random token substitutions in GPT-2; their behavioral effects are consistent across all six tested checkpoints. Our results show that robustness claims based on a single behavioral or representational metric can be misleading, and motivate multi-level evaluation of how perturbations alter language-model computation.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how different types of input noise affect language models not just in outputs but also in internal representations and attention behavior, showing that robustness looks different depending on what you measure.
AI.motivation: Robustness of language models is typically judged only by whether outputs change under noisy inputs, but this can miss substantial internal disruptions or overstate robustness. The authors aim to systematically characterize how various realistic and synthetic input perturbations propagate through models at multiple levels of computation.
AI.method: They apply six types of input perturbations (including typos, corrupted text, token substitutions, shuffling, and gradient-guided HotFlip) to several decoder-only language models: four GPT-2 checkpoints and two Qwen2.5 checkpoints. They evaluate effects on (1) output behavior (e.g., copying scores), (2) hidden-state geometry using metrics like centered kernel alignment and intrinsic dimension across layers, and (3) attention-head behavior in GPT-2, including activation patching, to see how specific heads respond to noise.
AI.result: Different perturbation types induce clearly distinguishable patterns across behavioral and representational metrics, and these patterns are not fully predictable from output behavior alone and are only partially consistent across model checkpoints. Copying behavior is strongly linked to the ability of activation patching to recover clean computations under token substitution and shuffling. Gradient-based HotFlip perturbations disrupt both behavior and representations more than random substitutions with the same corruption rate in GPT-2, and their behavioral impact generalizes across all six tested models.
AI.conclusion: Relying on a single robustness metric—either output-based or representation-based—can give a distorted picture of how robust a language model actually is. Robustness should instead be evaluated multi-level, incorporating outputs, internal geometry, and attention-level analysis to better understand how input perturbations alter model computation and where different models are vulnerable or resilient.

title: SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation, addressing the shortcomings of existing image-based metrics like CLIPScore when applied to vector graphics.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation metrics for generative models, especially CLIP-based scores, are designed for natural images and do not capture the typical errors and properties of SVGs, such as colors, object counts, and spatial relations. This mismatch hinders progress in text-to-SVG generation because model improvements cannot be reliably measured or compared.
AI.method: 1) Empirically analyze how current CLIP-based metrics and off-the-shelf VLM judges react to controlled perturbations in captions and SVGs, showing their insensitivity or uneven sensitivity to key SVG error types. 2) Construct a human-annotated dataset focused on Semantic Alignment between text prompts and generated SVGs. 3) Develop two evaluators: (a) CLIP-based scorers adapted to vector graphics and further aligned to human preference data for efficient large-scale scoring; (b) a VLM-based judge trained via supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning to provide richer, more interpretable assessments. 4) Use these evaluators to benchmark a range of SVG generators (open-source, commercial, and optimization-based) on a separate caption set.
AI.result: The authors show that standard CLIP scores are largely insensitive to realistic SVG generation errors and that generic VLM judges exhibit inconsistent behavior across error types and SVG styles. Their adapted and human-aligned CLIP scorers more closely track human judgments at scale, while the fine-tuned RL-shaped VLM judge captures nuanced semantic alignment properties. Together, these evaluators enable more reliable, discriminative benchmarking of different text-to-SVG generation systems.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific, human-aligned evaluation is crucial for advancing text-to-SVG generation. By providing a semantic alignment dataset and two complementary evaluators tailored to vector graphics, the paper offers a practical protocol and tools that better reflect human judgment than repurposed natural-image metrics, and can serve as a standard benchmark for future SVG generation work.

title: Less Is Moral: A CHARMing Framework for Moral Foundations Detection in Endorsement Behaviour
summary: Moral language plays a central role in shaping online endorsement and the diffusion of information, yet existing moral foundation detection systems often suffer from poor cross-domain generalization, weak rationale grounding, and reliance on costly prompting-based large language models (LLMs). We introduce CHARM, a MA\textbf{C}- and \textbf{H}ate-speech-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{R}ationale-aligned \textbf{M}oral foundation detection framework built on a lightweight fine-tuned LLM, which integrates complementary moral grounding, rationale alignment, and polarity-aware hate speech signals to support more robust and faithful moral prediction. Unlike prior dictionary-, fine-tune-, or prompt-based detectors, which decouple computation from psychological theory, CHARM is built so that each component -- MAC cross-attention, rationale alignment, and hate-speech modulation -- operationalizes a distinct psychological construct. Using a 30\% subsample of the MFTC, MFRC, and News training pools together with the richer supervision in MFTCXplain, CHARM improves AUC by up to 15.3\% in-domain, surpasses the supervised baselines on every out-of-domain dataset in both AUC and F1, and offers a scalable, low-cost alternative to prompting-based LLM detectors. We further apply CHARM to large-scale COVID-19 discourse on Twitter and show that moral value alignment is strongly associated with online endorsement behavior. By making moral framing measurable at scale, CHARM offers a practical tool for studying the spread of morally charged misinformation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CHARM, a lightweight, fine-tuned LLM framework for detecting moral foundations that better generalizes across domains, grounds predictions in rationales, and incorporates hate-speech signals, outperforming prior methods and enabling large-scale analysis of moral framing in online discourse.
AI.motivation: Existing moral foundation detection systems struggle with cross-domain generalization, provide weak or absent rationales, and often depend on expensive prompt-based large language models, limiting their reliability and scalability for studying moral language and misinformation online.
AI.method: The authors propose CHARM, a MAC- and hate-speech-aware rationale-aligned moral foundation detection framework built on a fine-tuned lightweight LLM. CHARM integrates three key components—MAC cross-attention for moral grounding, a rationale alignment mechanism to tie predictions to explicit textual rationales, and polarity-aware hate-speech modulation to account for hateful content—each designed to correspond to specific psychological constructs. They train CHARM using a 30% subsample of established moral datasets (MFTC, MFRC, News) plus the richer supervision of MFTCXplain.
AI.result: CHARM improves AUC by up to 15.3% on in-domain datasets, surpasses supervised baselines on all out-of-domain datasets in both AUC and F1, and operates as a scalable, low-cost alternative to prompting-based LLM detectors. Applied to large-scale COVID-19 Twitter data, CHARM reveals a strong association between moral value alignment in messages and online endorsement behavior.
AI.conclusion: By combining moral grounding, rationale alignment, and hate-speech-aware signals in a lightweight, fine-tuned LLM, CHARM achieves more robust and faithful moral foundation detection than prior approaches. This makes moral framing measurable at scale and provides a practical tool for analyzing how morally framed and potentially misleading information spreads online.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab is a causal, modality-agnostic collaborative perception framework that maps heterogeneous sensors into a unified protocol space, disentangles semantics from modality-specific noise, and achieves SOTA performance, especially when sensor modality gaps are large.
AI.motivation: Existing collaborative perception systems struggle in real-world deployments because different agents use heterogeneous sensors (e.g., LiDAR, camera, radar) and different model architectures. Protocol-based two-stage methods try to handle this by mapping each modality into a shared protocol space, but their converters are trained independently, so each modality still induces its own pseudo-protocol distribution. This leads to semantic inconsistency, error accumulation during collaboration, and especially poor performance when modalities differ greatly. The authors are motivated to design a unified, causal, and modality-agnostic framework that produces semantically consistent protocol representations across diverse modalities and can easily integrate new ones.
AI.method: The paper proposes CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network for collaborative perception. It formulates representation learning in the shared protocol space from a causal perspective: semantic factors are separated from modality-specific statistical confounders using causal metric learning. This encourages the protocol features to capture modality-invariant semantics. In parallel, a context-guided Unified Converter is introduced to convert heterogeneous modality features (from different sensors and architectures) into this shared space while enforcing cross-modal semantic consistency. The design allows new modalities to be integrated by training lightweight adapter modules rather than retraining the whole system.
AI.result: CauseCollab is evaluated on two multi-agent perception benchmarks, OPV2V and DAIR-V2X. Across these datasets, it achieves state-of-the-art performance for collaborative perception tasks and shows particularly large improvements in settings where there are substantial gaps between sensor modalities. This indicates that the proposed causal, unified protocol space and unified converter better handle heterogeneous and discrepant modalities than prior protocol-based methods.
AI.conclusion: CauseCollab successfully addresses semantic inconsistency and error accumulation that arise when trying to map heterogeneous sensors into a shared protocol space in collaborative perception. By using causal metric learning to disentangle semantics from modality-specific confounders and a context-guided Unified Converter to ensure semantic consistency, it builds a modality-agnostic protocol representation that scales to new modalities via small adapters. The empirical results on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X validate that this design achieves and surpasses state-of-the-art performance, with the most significant gains seen where modality discrepancies are largest.

title: FPCO-Dialog: A Multi-Turn False-Premise Benchmark for Correction and Cooperation in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at EMNLP2026 Main Conference. For code and data, see https://github.com/lab-klc/FPCO-Dialog
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-turn settings where users may describe visual content with incorrect assumptions. Yet existing evaluations rarely isolate how models respond when the same visually grounded false premise persists across dialogue turns. We introduce FPCO-Dialog, a benchmark for evaluating correction and cooperation behavior in VLMs under repeated false premises. FPCO-Dialog contains 1,080 images and 10,800 question turns, stratified by visual complexity, object category, and false-premise class, and uses a 10-turn protocol in which a correct dialogue prefix is followed by repeated false-premise referring expressions. We evaluate 20 commercial and open-source VLMs with a model-agnostic protocol and CorrTP@K, a correction-rate metric over false-premise turns, scored by two independent detectors. FPCO-Dialog reveals substantial and persistent cross-model differences in aggregate correction tendency, model-specific turn-wise dynamics, and systematic variation across false-premise types under the benchmark's substitution distribution. The dataset, evaluation protocol, model outputs, detector labels, and code are available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FPCO-Dialog, a benchmark to test how vision-language models correct or cooperate when users repeatedly ask questions with the same visually false assumptions.
AI.motivation: Existing evals of vision-language models don’t isolate behavior under *repeated* visually grounded false premises in multi-turn dialogues. In practice, users often persist in their mistaken assumptions about an image, and we lack systematic ways to measure whether models correct those errors or go along with them across turns.
AI.method: They construct FPCO-Dialog, a dataset of 1,080 images and 10,800 dialogue turns. Each dialogue has 10 turns: the first turns form a correct “prefix,” followed by multiple turns where the user’s questions repeatedly contain the same false premise tied to the image. The data is stratified by visual complexity, object category, and type of false premise. They design a model-agnostic evaluation protocol and define CorrTP@K, a correction-rate metric computed over the false-premise turns. Two independent detectors automatically score whether each model response corrects or cooperates with the false premise. They then test 20 commercial and open-source VLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: The benchmark uncovers large and consistent differences between models in how often they correct false premises overall, how their correction/cooperation behavior changes over dialogue turns, and how sensitive they are to different categories of false premises under the designed substitution distribution. These differences persist across models and conditions, indicating systematic behavioral patterns rather than random variation.
AI.conclusion: FPCO-Dialog provides a fine-grained way to evaluate vision-language models’ responses to persistent visually grounded false premises in dialogue, revealing that current systems vary widely and systematically in correction behavior. The released dataset, protocol, outputs, labels, and code enable future work on developing and benchmarking safer, more reliable VLM dialogue behavior in the presence of user mistakes.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs), which merge knowledge graphs with probabilistic reasoning so agents can treat web knowledge as calibrated beliefs instead of crisp facts.
AI.motivation: Current knowledge graphs represent information as deterministic facts, while modern AI systems like large language models and autonomous agents reason in probabilistic terms. This mismatch leads to shallow integrations where knowledge graphs are just data sources rather than components of a unified reasoning system. The authors want a framework where web-scale structured data can be used as a coherent probabilistic world model for agents.
AI.method: Conceptual and architectural proposal: (1) Reinterpret knowledge graphs as carriers of beliefs, not just facts. (2) Use ontological axioms to specify prior distributions. (3) Update beliefs via Bayesian conditioning based on observations. (4) Model actions as interventions that modify the world and thus belief states. They illustrate the framework through example tasks (security decision, actuarial estimation, planning, and inference of unstated quantities) and identify necessary infrastructure: belief annotations over RDF 1.2, probabilistic entailment semantics, calibration layers, and agent communication protocols for sharing and disputing beliefs.
AI.result: The paper does not report empirical results; instead, it clarifies the capabilities that SBWMs would grant to agents, such as probabilistic interpretation of KG content, better decision-making under uncertainty, and the ability to infer quantities not explicitly stated in any document. It specifies design requirements and components needed to realize SBWMs within the Web ecosystem.
AI.conclusion: Integrating knowledge graphs with probabilistic reasoning via Semantic Bayesian World Models can transform the Web from a repository of crisp facts into a shared probabilistic world model. Achieving this will require new standards and tools: RDF-level belief annotations, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration mechanisms, and interoperable protocols enabling agents to exchange and contest calibrated beliefs.

title: Accountable AI with Grounded, Faithful, Consistent, Actionable Rationales: A Case Study in Clinical Trial Matching with VERDICT
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 46 pages, 6 figures, 28 tables. Code and prompts: https://github.com/stanford-oval/clinical-trial-matching
summary:
Accountability means a decision can be examined, justified, and contested. LLMs make this hard: fluent output may be ungrounded, incomplete, or unfaithful to the decision process. Achieving accountability requires verified rationales (how was the decision reached), assumptions (what was assumed rather than known), policy consistency (the same treatment for the same facts), and pivotal conditions (what would change the outcome). We introduce self-faithfulness as an automatic test of accountability: changing the pivotal conditions should change the decision.
  We examine accountable AI through clinical trial matching, a high-stakes task central to evidence-based medicine. Although LLM-based matchers match patients to trials reasonably accurately, they apply decision policies inconsistently and produce rationales that are unfaithful to their own decisions.
  We introduce VERDICT, an LLM-based agent that translates a decision task, its constraints, and its policy into Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT), then derives the decision with SMT and MaxSMT solvers -- so policies are applied consistently and decisions are accountable by construction.
  Across a SIGIR 2016-derived dataset and TREC 2021, VERDICT achieves the strongest decision accuracy among LLM-only and neurosymbolic baselines, applies policies with perfect consistency, and produces clinician-preferred rationales grounded in explicit assumptions and pivotal conditions, with improved counterfactual self-faithfulness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes VERDICT, a neurosymbolic LLM+SMT system to make AI decisions accountable and consistent in clinical trial matching, outperforming LLM-only baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs can match patients to clinical trials reasonably well but lack accountability: their rationales may be unfaithful, assumptions implicit, policies inconsistently applied, and decisions insensitive to stated pivotal conditions. In high-stakes domains like evidence-based medicine, stakeholders need decisions that can be examined, justified, contested, and subjected to counterfactual analysis, which current LLMs fail to guarantee.
AI.method: The authors formalize accountability requirements (verified rationales, explicit assumptions, policy consistency, pivotal conditions) and define self-faithfulness: altering pivotal conditions should alter decisions. They implement VERDICT, an LLM-based agent that converts the decision task, constraints, and policy for clinical trial matching into Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) and MaxSMT problems. The SMT solver then computes decisions, ensuring that policies are applied exactly and consistently. LLMs are used for translation and explanation, while the symbolic backbone enforces logical correctness. They evaluate VERDICT on a SIGIR 2016-derived dataset and TREC 2021, comparing to LLM-only and neurosymbolic baselines.
AI.result: VERDICT attains the highest decision accuracy among all evaluated systems on both datasets, enforces perfect policy consistency by construction, and generates rationales that clinicians prefer over those from baselines. These rationales are explicitly grounded in stated assumptions and pivotal conditions. VERDICT also exhibits better counterfactual behavior according to the self-faithfulness test: changing pivotal conditions more reliably leads to corresponding changes in decisions.
AI.conclusion: Embedding LLMs within an SMT-based decision framework can deliver accountable AI in high-stakes tasks. By separating policy enforcement (symbolic solver) from language understanding and explanation (LLM), VERDICT achieves both strong accuracy and formally consistent, self-faithful decisions and rationales. This approach suggests a viable path for trustworthy deployment of LLMs in domains like clinical trial matching and potentially other regulated decision-making settings.

title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a graph-constrained, agent-based LLM framework to adapt complex retail supply chain decision pipelines to new natural-language requirements, improving end-to-end success over direct LLM reformulation.
AI.motivation: Retail supply chain operations depend on multiple interconnected optimization and decision modules. As business requirements change, practitioners need to adapt these pipelines without deep technical knowledge. Current LLM approaches mainly handle single optimization models and do not address how to choose where and how to intervene in a heterogeneous pipeline when a requirement can be satisfied through different modification routes with varying downstream impact. There is thus a need for a systematic, requirement-driven method that can select effective intervention paths and translate natural-language requirements into consistent changes across modules.
AI.method: The authors formalize requirement-driven adaptation as a joint problem: selecting both an intervention route through a decision pipeline and a specific admissible change within targeted modules. They design a graph-constrained agentic framework where: (1) each domain agent corresponds to a module in the pipeline and exposes a restricted interface describing admissible reformulations; (2) a central processor performs a bounded search over possible intervention paths in the graph of modules; and (3) candidate adaptations are instantiated via LLMs and then evaluated using downstream KPIs from the operational system. The framework is instantiated using several base LLMs (GPT, Qwen, DeepSeek) and applied to real warehouse decision pipelines.
AI.result: In a collaborative study with a large retail partner, the authors collect 100 real warehouse requirements from practitioner interviews. They compare their framework against direct LLM reformulation of modules, across three base LLMs (GPT, Qwen, DeepSeek). The proposed method improves both correctness of the adaptations and overall end-to-end success. Quantitatively, end-to-end success rates increase from a baseline of 72–76% with direct LLM reformulation to 79–83% when using the graph-constrained agentic framework.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that structuring LLM-based adaptation via graph-constrained domain agents and bounded search over intervention paths yields more reliable modification of complex retail decision pipelines than direct, unconstrained LLM reformulation. By encoding admissible changes and validating candidates against downstream KPIs, the framework better aligns natural-language requirements with operational constraints, providing a practical path to deploy LLMs as controllers for real-world, heterogeneous supply chain decision systems.

title: FrameBench:A Language Understanding Benchmark Based on Frame Semantics
summary: In frame semantics, sentence comprehension is assumed to proceed by relating lexical meaning to background knowledge called semantic frames, thereby enabling readers to implicitly enrich the text with unstated information. Recent large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of downstream tasks. However, it remains unclear whether they can reproduce the kinds of implicit enrichment that humans naturally make during comprehension. To address this question, we introduce FrameBench, a benchmark grounded in frame semantics. FrameBench consists of multiple-choice questions that test whether models distinguish the frames evoked by the same verb across contexts. We construct the benchmark for English and Japanese using FrameNet-style resources and a generation-and-verification pipeline with native-speaker judgments. Our experiments on a diverse set of models reveal challenges for small models, while several large models surpass the human reference scores. We release the constructed FrameBench dataset and the code for dataset construction and evaluation at https://github.com/SasanoLab/FrameBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FrameBench, a benchmark to test whether language models can distinguish verb-evoked semantic frames across contexts in English and Japanese, showing small models struggle while several large models exceed human performance.
AI.motivation: While frame semantics suggests humans enrich text by linking words to background knowledge (semantic frames), it is unknown whether large language models can perform similar implicit enrichment, especially distinguishing different frames evoked by the same verb in varying contexts.
AI.method: The authors create FrameBench, a multiple-choice benchmark built from FrameNet-style resources in English and Japanese. They use a generation-and-verification pipeline that incorporates native-speaker judgments to construct questions testing whether models pick the correct frame for a verb in context. They then evaluate a broad range of models on this benchmark and compare their performance with human reference scores.
AI.result: Experiments show that smaller language models face significant difficulties in correctly distinguishing verb frames across contexts, while several large language models perform strongly and even surpass human reference scores on the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: FrameBench effectively probes LLMs’ ability to perform frame-semantic interpretation, revealing a performance gap between small and large models and indicating that some large LLMs may match or even exceed humans in this specific type of implicit semantic enrichment. The dataset and accompanying code are publicly released to support further research.

title: Bioinfoysis Technical Report
summary: Large language model agents have shown promise in bioinformatics, but most existing systems focus primarily on producing final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as transient interactions. This design is poorly suited to long-horizon bioinformatics tasks, where conclusions must remain connected to the data, computations, and intermediate evidence that support them. We introduce \textbf{Bioinfoysis}, a multi-agent harness that represents each request as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run. Bioinfoysis combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning: the planner maintains an executable checklist and revises pending steps using structured handoffs returned after each worker execution. These handoffs bind intermediate results to their responsible agent, checklist step, and plan generation, preventing stale evidence from being silently reused after replanning. A controlled runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures before they are used in downstream analysis or reporting, while role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills support reliable execution over long analysis trajectories. We evaluate Bioinfoysis on BixBench and two question-answering tracks of LAB-Bench 2. On BixBench, Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4\%. Across four underlying language models, Bioinfoysis increases average accuracy from 27.81\% to 64.13\% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13\% to 31.25\% on DbQA2. These results demonstrate that reliable bioinformatics automation depends not only on model capability, but also on the harness that governs planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. We hope that the emergence of Bioinfoysis will play a driving and leading role in the development of the bioinformatics community. Our demo website can be seen in https://report.bioinfoysis.com/.

AI.tldr: Bioinfoysis is a multi-agent LLM harness for bioinformatics that treats each task as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run, integrating planning, validated tool use, and evidence tracking to greatly improve accuracy on long-horizon benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based bioinformatics agents mainly aim to produce final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as temporary steps. This is inadequate for complex, long-horizon analyses where final conclusions must remain tightly linked to the underlying data, code, and intermediate results. There is a need for a system that maintains persistent, verifiable analysis traces and prevents the use of outdated or unverified evidence while still leveraging LLM capabilities.
AI.method: The authors design Bioinfoysis, a multi-agent framework where each request becomes a persistent analysis run grounded in concrete artifacts (scripts, tables, figures, logs). A global planner maintains an executable checklist of steps and performs evidence-driven replanning as worker agents execute tasks. Structured handoffs bind intermediate results to their originating agent, checklist item, and plan version, so that stale evidence is invalidated after replanning. A controlled runtime automatically validates generated scripts and outputs before they are consumed downstream. Role-specific contexts, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills are used to support reliable, long-running bioinformatics workflows across different underlying language models.
AI.result: On the BixBench benchmark, Bioinfoysis attains state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4%. On the SeqQA2 and DbQA2 tracks from LAB-Bench 2, using four different underlying LLMs, Bioinfoysis boosts average accuracy from 27.81% to 64.13% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13% to 31.25% on DbQA2. These gains demonstrate substantial improvements over vanilla LLM usage across multiple models and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Reliability in automated bioinformatics analysis is determined not only by the underlying language model, but critically by the surrounding harness that manages planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. By grounding analyses in persistent artifacts, enforcing validation, and carefully coordinating multi-agent planning and execution, Bioinfoysis substantially improves performance on challenging benchmarks and offers a promising direction for robust, long-horizon bioinformatics automation.

title: Chiaroscuro for Emotions: A Contrastive Emotion Benchmark Grounded in Appraisal Theory
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference) Dataset and code: https://github.com/cincynlp/Chiaro
summary: Emotion recognition benchmarks often predict one emotion per text, missing many real-world scenarios where two people arrive at opposing emotions from a single shared event. For example, a child kicks the seat in front of her in excitement while the passenger ahead grows angry. We introduce CHIARO, a 1,000 human-annotated sentence benchmark for contrastive emotion inference grounded in appraisal theory. Each scene describes one causal trigger eliciting a positive emotion in one person and a negative emotion in the other, drawn from a ten-class taxonomy. We benchmark seven frontier LLMs and four off-the-shelf emotion classifiers. The strongest LLM reaches 67.3 macro-F1, well below human agreement, while existing emotion classifiers score near chance. Beyond evaluation, CHIARO also serves as a training signal. When combined with an existing emotion corpus, the resulting downstream classifier improves on CHIARO itself and on six of ten external emotion benchmarks, which positions our dataset as a complementary signal for emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CHIARO, a new benchmark for contrastive emotion inference where a single event elicits opposite emotions in two people, and shows current LLMs and emotion classifiers perform far below human level.
AI.motivation: Most emotion recognition benchmarks assume a single emotion label per text, overlooking real-world situations where different people experience contrasting emotions from the same event. The authors aim to fill this gap by creating a dataset grounded in appraisal theory that explicitly models such contrastive emotional responses.
AI.method: They construct CHIARO, a dataset of 1,000 human-annotated sentences, each depicting one causal trigger that simultaneously generates a positive emotion in one person and a negative emotion in another, using a ten-class taxonomy of emotions. They then benchmark seven frontier large language models and four existing emotion classifiers on this dataset. Finally, they use CHIARO as additional training data alongside an existing emotion corpus to train a downstream classifier, and evaluate its performance on CHIARO and ten external emotion benchmarks.
AI.result: The best-performing LLM achieves a macro-F1 score of 67.3, still well below human inter-annotator agreement, and off-the-shelf emotion classifiers perform near chance on the CHIARO benchmark. When CHIARO is used as a training signal in combination with an existing emotion corpus, the resulting classifier improves performance both on CHIARO and on six out of ten external emotion benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: CHIARO exposes a challenging dimension of emotion understanding—contrastive emotions triggered by the same event—that current models handle poorly. At the same time, incorporating CHIARO into training improves general emotion recognition, indicating that contrastive-emotion data is a valuable and complementary signal for advancing emotion understanding in NLP models.

title: STAIR (STructure Aware Information Retriever): A novel dataset and LLM based retriever for document structure augmentation
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a key component for generating accurate and hallucination free answers using Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are improving at handling long context, but still suffer from "lost in the middle" problem. Thus, precise and accurate retrieval is important. Current retrievers chunk long context into length-based manageable chunks - in the process throwing away rich and informative semantic global structure in the corpus. We introduce a novel retrieval system STAIR that empowers an LLM to exploit global structure in a corpus such as a Table of Contents (ToC) to efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Our thorough and careful ablation studies with a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system show that ToC helps build a low hallucination (less than 0.05%) generative Information Retrieval (IR) system and can generalize to examples where very few training samples are available. To further research in this novel direction of ToC based retrieval we release SearchTome - a diverse benchmark created from 18 books across 6 diverse domains to further research in this novel direction. STAIR achieves a high Recall@1 score of 82.6% on SearchTome as compared to DSI (76.9%), where the difference is found to be statistically significant. STAIR easily beats other strong baselines such as BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%) and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes STAIR, a retrieval system that leverages global corpus structure (like tables of contents) to improve Retrieval-Augmented Generation, showing higher recall and lower hallucinations than existing retrievers on a new benchmark, SearchTome.
AI.motivation: Standard retrieval for RAG splits documents into length-based chunks, losing global semantic structure and leading to suboptimal retrieval and hallucinations, especially given LLMs’ limitations with long context and the “lost in the middle” issue. The authors aim to exploit natural global structure such as tables of contents to guide retrieval and storage, improving accuracy, robustness with few training samples, and hallucination control.
AI.method: They introduce STAIR, a retrieval system that conditions a Differentiable Search Index (DSI)-style model on global corpus structure, particularly Tables of Contents, so the model can map queries to relevant document sections using this hierarchy. They perform careful ablation studies to isolate the effect of ToC information, fine-tune DSI models with ToC-augmented signals, and compare against traditional and neural retrievers. They also construct the SearchTome benchmark from 18 books in 6 domains to evaluate ToC-based retrieval. Metrics such as Recall@1 and hallucination rates are used.
AI.result: On the SearchTome benchmark, STAIR achieves Recall@1 of 82.6%, significantly outperforming a vanilla DSI (76.9%), and beating other baselines like BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%), and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%). Ablation studies show that incorporating ToC information substantially reduces hallucination rates, achieving under 0.05%, and improves generalization in low-data regimes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating global corpus structure, especially tables of contents, into retrieval systems meaningfully improves retrieval quality and reduces hallucinations in RAG settings. STAIR demonstrates that ToC-guided retrieval outperforms both traditional sparse and dense retrievers and even strong LLM baselines. The newly released SearchTome benchmark provides a standardized way to study and advance ToC-based retrieval and structure-aware IR systems.

title: TabScope: Question-Adaptive Scope Selection for Table Question Answering
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on table question answering, yet their accuracy often degrades as table size increases. We find that this degradation is not uniform across question types. Localization-sensitive questions are particularly affected by irrelevant table content, while questions requiring broader evidence may still benefit from full-table reasoning. Based on this observation, we propose a question-adaptive framework that dynamically selects between localized and full-table reasoning. The framework constructs question-specific sub-tables through operation-aware table decomposition and uses the predicted question type to determine the appropriate reasoning mode. We further introduce silver reference sub-tables for evaluating evidence selection and construct SLQA, a benchmark based on real-world long tables. Experiments on WikiTQ and SLQA show that localization is particularly effective for lookup and local reasoning questions, while adaptive selection between localized and full-table reasoning achieves the best overall performance. These results highlight that long-table QA requires deciding not only how to localize, but also when to localize. Our code and datasets will be made available upon publication of the paper.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a question-adaptive framework for table question answering on long tables that dynamically chooses between localized and full-table reasoning to maintain accuracy as table size grows.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well on table QA but their accuracy drops as tables get larger, especially for certain question types. Existing approaches often either always use full-table reasoning (which adds noise and cost) or always localize (which can drop necessary evidence). The authors observe that different question types are differently affected by irrelevant content: localization-sensitive questions suffer most, while questions that need broad evidence may still benefit from full-table access. This motivates a framework that can adapt its reasoning strategy per question.
AI.method: The framework first performs operation-aware table decomposition to build question-specific sub-tables, essentially extracting only the relevant parts of a long table for a given query. It then predicts the question type (e.g., lookup, local reasoning, broader reasoning) and, based on that prediction, dynamically chooses a reasoning mode: either localized reasoning over the constructed sub-table or full-table reasoning over the entire table. To evaluate evidence selection quality, the authors introduce silver reference sub-tables—automatically constructed approximations of gold evidence sets. They also build SLQA, a new benchmark of real-world long tables aimed at testing long-table QA and evidence localization.
AI.result: On WikiTQ and the new SLQA benchmark, localized reasoning is shown to significantly boost performance for lookup and local reasoning questions, which are especially harmed by irrelevant table content. However, for questions requiring more global or aggregated evidence, full-table reasoning remains beneficial. The question-adaptive system that switches between localized and full-table modes based on predicted question type achieves the highest overall accuracy across question types and datasets, outperforming single-strategy baselines.
AI.conclusion: Long-table QA is not just about how to localize relevant content but also about when to localize it. A question-adaptive framework that can select between localized and full-table reasoning per question leads to better performance than always-localized or always-full-table approaches. The introduced evaluation tools (silver reference sub-tables and SLQA) further support systematic study of evidence selection and reasoning over long tables.

title: Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
summary:
We introduce Xiaomi-TabLDM, a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression via in-context learning, which delivers superior prediction accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs), our model enables more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.
  i) A new performance standard. Strong regression performance across benchmarks: Xiaomi-TabLDM ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO, demonstrating consistently strong regression performance across four complementary benchmark suites. Favorable performance--efficiency trade-off: Xiaomi-TabLDM combines strong predictive performance with substantially lower computational cost. For example, on TabArena regression, it achieves the second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
  ii) Large-scale synthetic pretraining. Xiaomi-TabLDM expands the coverage and diversity of synthetic tabular data used for pretraining. We also adopt a three-stage training strategy together with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts, enabling Xiaomi-TabLDM to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization across diverse tabular tasks.
  iii) Test-time scaling. Xiaomi-TabLDM further extends tabular prediction through test-time compute scaling, where allocating additional computation at inference time consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-TabLDM is a tabular foundation model that uses large-scale synthetic pretraining and test-time compute scaling to achieve top-tier regression and strong classification performance via in-context learning, without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional tabular models either require task-specific training or fail to generalize broadly without fine-tuning, and existing tabular foundation models are often computationally expensive or limited in data diversity. The authors aim to build a single, general tabular model that attains state-of-the-art performance on diverse benchmarks, scales efficiently, and can be applied directly via in-context learning rather than retraining.
AI.method: The paper proposes Xiaomi-TabLDM, a large data foundation model for tabular classification and regression that operates via in-context learning. It is pretrained solely on large-scale synthetic tabular datasets generated from structural causal models (SCMs), with expanded coverage and diversity. The training uses a three-stage curriculum and architectural components such as dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual modules, and a sparse Mixture-of-Experts design to better learn feature interactions and specialized experts. At inference, the model supports test-time compute scaling: allocating more computation (e.g., more passes or expert usage) improves performance without retraining.
AI.result: Across multiple public benchmark suites (OpenML-CTR23, TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO), Xiaomi-TabLDM achieves state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art regression performance, ranking 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on the combined regression benchmarks. It also provides a favorable performance–efficiency trade-off, such as reaching the second-highest Elo score on TabArena regression while using about 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the best TabFM baseline. Test-time compute scaling consistently boosts performance beyond the base model.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic pretraining on diverse SCM-generated tabular data, coupled with specialized architectural design and test-time compute scaling, can produce a single tabular foundation model that performs competitively or better than task-specific models on a wide range of regression (and likely classification) tasks. Xiaomi-TabLDM shows that strong tabular in-context learning is possible without real-data pretraining or task-specific fine-tuning, offering both accuracy and computational efficiency and setting a new performance standard for tabular foundation models.

title: To What Extent Do Large Language Models Understand Bangla Idioms?
summary: Idiomatic expressions are an integral part of natural language, reflecting cultural nuances and posing unique challenges for computational models, particularly in low-resource languages. In this paper, we present the first large-scale benchmark dataset of Bangla idioms, complemented by a synthetic multiple-choice question (MCQ) dataset for idiom meaning identification. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of recent large language models (LLMs) across three idiom-related tasks: paraphrasing, idiom span detection, and meaning identification, leveraging zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variability in model performance, with no single LLM consistently outperforming others across all tasks. Notably, Phi-4-mini-instruct excels in paraphrasing, Kimi-K2-32b-instruct in span detection, and Gemini-2.5-flash in meaning identification. We believe that our datasets and analyses will provide valuable resources to guide future research in improving LLM comprehension of idiomatic expressions, particularly in Bangla and other low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: They build the first large-scale Bangla idiom benchmark plus an MCQ dataset, and test various LLMs on paraphrasing, idiom detection, and meaning identification, showing mixed strengths across models.
AI.motivation: Idioms are culturally rich and hard for models to handle, especially in low-resource languages like Bangla, where there is a lack of dedicated large-scale resources and benchmarks for idiomatic expressions. This gap hinders systematic evaluation and improvement of LLMs on idiom understanding.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale dataset of Bangla idioms and a synthetic multiple-choice dataset for idiom meaning identification. They then evaluate several recent LLMs on three tasks—idiom paraphrasing, idiom span detection in text, and meaning identification—using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, comparing model performance across tasks.
AI.result: They observe significant variation in LLM performance across the three idiom-related tasks, with no single model dominating. Phi-4-mini-instruct performs best on paraphrasing, Kimi-K2-32b-instruct performs best on idiom span detection, and Gemini-2.5-flash performs best on meaning identification.
AI.conclusion: The new Bangla idiom benchmark and MCQ dataset fill a key resource gap and show that current LLMs have uneven strengths in idiom comprehension. These resources and findings can guide future work to better model idioms in Bangla and, by extension, other low-resource languages.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a fully deterministic artificial agent, designed with an affect-like system that models uncertainty about its internal needs and external resources, can display hedonic place preference behavior similar to that seen in animals, raising questions about what this implies for consciousness and free will.
AI.motivation: Many scientists treat hedonic place preference—seeking locations associated with non-nutritional rewards like drugs—as evidence that animals have conscious feelings, because such behavior seems hard to explain as purely instinctive or unconscious. The authors want to challenge and refine this assumption by asking whether similar behavior can emerge in a simple, fully deterministic artificial system, and what that means for claims about the physical basis of consciousness and free will.
AI.method: They conceptually design and/or implement a simple artificial agent that includes an affect-like control system. This system represents the agent’s intrinsic needs, its uncertainty about how environmental resources can satisfy those needs, and uses that uncertainty in its information processing and decision-making. The agent is placed in an environment where it can learn associations between locations and ‘pleasure-producing’ but non-nutritional rewards, and its behavior is analyzed to see whether hedonic place preference emerges.
AI.result: The artificial agent, despite being fully deterministic, exhibits hedonic place preference behavior: it spends more time in locations associated with non-nutritional, reward-like stimuli in a way that resembles animals’ attraction to drugs or other pleasure-inducing substances. Its internal processing can be interpreted as a sort of subjective evaluation or felt uncertainty about needs and resources, even though it is mechanistically specified.
AI.conclusion: The existence of hedonic place preference in a simple deterministic agent suggests that such behavior alone cannot be taken as strong evidence of consciousness or genuine subjective feelings. Instead, hedonic preference can arise from particular computational/physical architectures of need representation and uncertainty management. This has implications for theories that infer consciousness or free will from patterns of goal-directed, reward-seeking behavior, and it supports the idea that aspects of what we call ‘feeling’ and ‘choice’ might be realizable in fully deterministic systems.

title: Lngram v2: Latent N-Gram Memory with Interpretable Discrete Representations
summary: Transformers lack a native lookup mechanism, requiring repeated dense computation to recognize and reuse local static patterns. Lngram v1 introduces tokenizer-independent conditional memory through discrete latent n-gram addressing, but its memory capacity is coupled with the backbone width, limiting scalability due to high parameter and activation costs. We propose Lngram v2, which decouples the number of routes, memory dimension, and backbone width, and introduces a context-aware grouped-query attention readout to scale memory capacity independently. A zero-value Sink and counterfactual surrogate gradients further improve readout selectivity and routing trainability while preserving hard discrete addressing. Experiments across vision--language models (VLMs) of different scales show consistent improvements, including successful scaling to a 30B-parameter model. Compared with Lngram v1, Lngram v2 substantially reduces both total and activated memory parameters while maintaining or improving language modeling performance. Further analysis shows that its discrete IDs preserve substantial semantic structure of continuous hidden states, enabling semantic recovery from IDs alone and stable ID--semantic associations across datasets. These results establish Lngram v2 as an efficient and scalable latent conditional memory mechanism whose discrete addresses also provide a structured interface for analyzing internal model representations.

AI.tldr: Lngram v2 is an improved, scalable discrete memory mechanism for Transformers that decouples memory capacity from model width, reduces parameter/activation cost, and keeps semantically meaningful discrete addresses.
AI.motivation: Transformers lack an efficient native mechanism to look up and reuse local static patterns, forcing them to repeatedly recompute the same dense operations. Lngram v1 introduced a discrete latent n-gram memory to address this, but its capacity scaled with backbone width, making it expensive in parameters and activations and hard to scale to large models. The motivation is to design a conditional memory mechanism that scales memory capacity independently of backbone size, is trainable with hard discrete addressing, and remains efficient in both parameters and compute while giving interpretable internal structure.
AI.method: The paper proposes Lngram v2, which decouples three factors: number of memory routes, memory dimension, and backbone width. It introduces a context-aware grouped-query attention readout to enable large memory capacity independent of the backbone. A dedicated zero-value Sink slot and counterfactual surrogate gradients are used to sharpen selectivity of readout and improve routing trainability, while keeping the addressing itself hard and discrete. The model assigns discrete n-gram IDs as latent memory addresses and uses the new readout mechanism to retrieve content from these addresses during Transformer computation. The method is evaluated across vision–language models (VLMs) of different scales, including up to 30B parameters, and includes analyses of the semantic structure encoded in the discrete IDs.
AI.result: Across VLMs of various sizes, Lngram v2 consistently improves performance relative to baselines and successfully scales to a 30B-parameter model. Compared with Lngram v1, Lngram v2 substantially reduces both the total number of memory parameters and the number of parameters that are activated per use, while maintaining or improving language modeling performance. Additional analysis shows that the learned discrete IDs retain a strong mapping to the underlying continuous hidden states, such that semantic information can be partially reconstructed from the IDs alone and that ID–semantic relationships remain stable across different datasets.
AI.conclusion: Lngram v2 provides an efficient and scalable latent conditional memory for Transformers, overcoming Lngram v1’s coupling between memory capacity and backbone width. Its decoupled design and context-aware grouped-query readout allow large memory capacity with fewer parameters and lower activation cost, while zero Sink and surrogate gradients improve trainability and selectivity under hard discrete addressing. The discrete memory IDs form a structured, semantically meaningful interface that can be used to analyze and interpret internal model representations, positioning Lngram v2 as both a practical and analytically useful memory mechanism.

title: Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans
summary: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

AI.tldr: The paper extends classical plan deordering techniques to Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning to reduce unnecessary ordering constraints in HTN plans.
AI.motivation: While HTN planning is a strong formalism based on task decomposition, most work has focused on generating plans rather than optimizing them afterwards. Specifically, plan deordering—well-studied in classical planning to increase flexibility by removing superfluous orderings—has not been thoroughly explored in HTN planning, where hierarchical decomposition adds extra constraints.
AI.method: The authors adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning to the HTN setting by extending them to respect hierarchical decomposition constraints. They implement these techniques and apply them as post-processing to HTN plans produced for the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmark domains, and compare their deordered plans against Optiplan, an HTN planner that directly outputs partially ordered plans.
AI.result: Both adapted deordering methods substantially reduce the number of ordering constraints in HTN plans compared to the original plans and to Optiplan’s partially ordered plans. The deordering also reduces the plans’ critical path length, though this improvement is more modest than the reduction in ordering constraints.
AI.conclusion: Classical deordering methods can be successfully transferred to HTN planning if they are extended to handle hierarchical decomposition constraints. This post-plan optimization significantly increases plan flexibility by cutting many unnecessary orderings, with some benefit in execution time (critical path), suggesting that deordering is a valuable but underused optimization step in HTN planning pipelines.

title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Large language models achieve superior performance on tasks that require extended reasoning, but long chains of thought make the KV cache a severe memory bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods share one paradigm: score each cached token by some estimate of how much it will matter later, and keep the top-scoring ones. We show that the selection signal contributes almost nothing. Random Attention keeps the prompt and evicts uniformly at random within each attention head, computing no score at all; across four models and six reasoning tasks it matches the strongest prior evictor while serving 32-43% higher throughput than it in vLLM deployment. Controlled experiments explain this by showing that 1) the prompt is the fragile part of the cache, and most of the gap between selectors is just whether their selection signal happened to keep it; 2) the reasoning trace protects itself against eviction with redundancy at two levels, in the text (the model restates what it still needs as it works) and across attention heads (each keeps its own copy of the trace), so once the prompt is safe, a random draw retains enough copies of what the model still needs, and no score is required to pick them. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/Random-Attention.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that random eviction of KV-cache entries, while always preserving the original prompt, matches or outperforms sophisticated KV-cache compression methods for long reasoning tasks, yielding much higher throughput.
AI.motivation: Long chains of thought in large language models require large KV caches, becoming a severe memory bottleneck during inference, especially for deployment systems like vLLM. Existing compression methods are complex and rely on heuristic scoring of token importance, and it is unclear how necessary this sophistication is.
AI.method: The authors propose Random Attention: always keep the initial prompt tokens and, within each attention head, evict cached tokens uniformly at random instead of using any importance score. They evaluate this scheme against state-of-the-art KV cache selection/eviction methods across four LLMs and six extended reasoning benchmarks in a vLLM deployment setup. They also run controlled ablation experiments to identify which parts of the cache are most fragile and how redundancy in reasoning traces affects robustness to eviction.
