These results show that evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FLY-EVAL++, a safety- and physics-aware evaluation protocol for large language models in safety-critical, physics-governed tasks, showing that conventional accuracy metrics miss crucial safety and feasibility failures.
AI.motivation: Standard LLM evaluation in safety-critical, physics-based domains (like aviation) relies heavily on accuracy or numerical closeness to ground truth. However, predictions can be numerically accurate yet violate safety constraints, physical laws, or required structured formats, making them operationally unusable or dangerous. Existing protocols do not systematically capture these failure modes, creating a gap between benchmark performance and real-world reliability.
AI.method: The authors propose FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven evaluation protocol that (1) deterministically verifies protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints; and (2) aggregates these checks into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores via a fixed rubric. They instantiate this framework on Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench benchmark with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks, and then apply FLY-EVAL++ to evaluate 66 LLMs.
AI.result: When applied to 66 LLMs, FLY-EVAL++ reveals that safety compliance is the most discriminative behavioral dimension: models with similar predictive accuracy can differ by more than 28 points in safety score. The study uncovers systematic issues such as safety violations even under physically plausible trajectories and instability during multi-step rollouts, which accuracy metrics alone would not highlight.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that evaluation protocols for LLMs in safety-critical, physics-governed domains must explicitly measure constraint satisfaction (safety, physical feasibility) and structured output validity. Accuracy-centric reporting alone is insufficient and can mask critical failure modes, so future benchmarks should adopt richer, constraint-aware evaluation schemes like FLY-EVAL++.

title: </think> Doesn't Stop Reasoning: Analysis of Spurious CoT Termination
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning improves large reasoning models (LRMs) on complex tasks but often produces long, redundant traces. Recent training-free early-exit methods shorten these traces by choosing an intermediate point to stop reasoning. We study one such strategy that injects an end-of-think token (EoT, </think>) at this point to trigger the reasoning-to-answering transition, and find that the injected EoT does not always induce a clean answering phase. Answering-phase generation can continue before the model regenerates another EoT, with the span preceding this regenerated EoT scaling with the reasoning tokens saved by early exit and exhibiting continued reasoning behavior. We call this spurious CoT termination, where reasoning-like generation continues into the answering phase. We hypothesize that insufficient attention to the injected EoT contributes to spurious CoT termination and probe this hypothesis with Exit-token Attention Biasing (EAB). Across four LRMs, five benchmarks, and two early-exit methods, increasing attention to the injected EoT reduces spurious CoT termination and answering-phase length. These results reveal a limitation of controlling LRMs by externally matching their explicit think-block format. Inserting the EoT token conforms to this format but does not by itself guarantee the intended reasoning-to-answering transition. Our code is available at https://github.com/Seunghee-Koh/Spurious-CoT-Termination.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that simply injecting an end-of-think token to stop chain-of-thought is unreliable: models often keep reasoning in the "answer" segment. By biasing attention toward this exit token, spurious extra reasoning and answer length are reduced.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought improves reasoning but leads to long, inefficient traces. Training-free early-exit methods aim to shorten these traces by inserting an end-of-think token, assuming it forces a transition from reasoning to answering. However, practitioners lack understanding of whether this control mechanism truly cleanly separates reasoning from answering and what failure modes arise when it does not.
AI.method: The authors empirically analyze large reasoning models using an injected end-of-think (EoT) token under existing early-exit strategies. They characterize the phenomenon they call spurious CoT termination, where reasoning-like behavior continues after the injected EoT and up to a later, regenerated EoT. They measure how this span scales with tokens saved by early exit, then propose Exit-token Attention Biasing (EAB), which explicitly increases the model's attention to the injected EoT. They evaluate EAB across four LRMs, five reasoning benchmarks, and two early-exit methods, comparing spurious CoT termination and answer-phase length with and without biasing.
AI.result: The study finds that injecting an EoT token does not reliably induce a clean switch from reasoning to answering; models often keep producing reasoning-like content during the supposed answering phase until they naturally regenerate another EoT. The length of this spurious reasoning segment grows with the amount of reasoning truncated by early exit. When they apply Exit-token Attention Biasing, attention to the injected EoT increases, which significantly reduces spurious CoT termination and shortens the answering phase across multiple models, benchmarks, and early-exit schemes.
AI.conclusion: Externally matching a model’s explicit think/answer format by inserting an EoT token is not enough to reliably control its internal reasoning-to-answering transition. The observed spurious CoT termination highlights a limitation of current training-free early-exit approaches. However, modifying the model’s attention to the exit token via EAB can mitigate this issue, suggesting that effective control of LRMs requires shaping attention dynamics in addition to structural token prompts.

title: Instruction Duplication as an Inference-Time Control Primitive
comment: 7 pages, 2 tables. Code and frozen reproduction artifacts: https://github.com/victorlavrenko/answer-engineering/releases/tag/instruction-duplication-arxiv-v1
summary: Procedural instruction following is a basic requirement for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. We introduce instruction duplication, a minimal black-box inference-time control that repeats only the procedural instruction, without retraining or decoding changes. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two copies raises the deterministic All-8 diagnostic--responses passing all eight observable tests--from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of the failures remaining after one copy. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rises from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 points; Holm-adjusted p < .001), while final-answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). A blinded challenge audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, and no reversals; its prespecified 28/30 confirmation criterion is not met. Yet this distinction can matter operationally when a downstream system acts on the generated trajectory. In Answer Engineering (AE), where explicit trajectory state determines local repair, the published reason-first no-editing SSNHL endpoint was 25.1%; system-only AE was later reproduced at 84.2%, and the same trailing duplicate raised it to 97.1%. For conductive diagnostic branch preservation, the corresponding values are 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% with reproduced AE, and 73.8% with AE plus duplication--a within-AE decrease, but still 14.9 points above the no-editing baseline. Instruction duplication is therefore a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value can emerge through the downstream system that consumes the exposed trajectory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a simple inference-time trick—duplicating the procedural instruction—to improve how reliably LLMs follow instructions without retraining, and shows modest but meaningful gains in several diagnostic metrics, especially when outputs feed into downstream “answer engineering” systems.
AI.motivation: Instruction-following reliability is crucial for controllable language models, particularly when intermediate reasoning trajectories are audited or automatically repaired downstream. Existing approaches often require retraining, complex decoding, or system redesign. The authors want a minimal, black-box method that can be applied at inference time to improve procedural adherence and the quality of trajectories, especially in safety-critical domains like medical multiple-choice questions.
AI.method: They introduce “instruction duplication”: repeating only the procedural instruction (not the entire prompt) once more in the input, with no model retraining and no change to decoding algorithms. They evaluate this across seven instruction-tuned LLMs on 300 medical multiple-choice questions, testing eight different placement conditions for the duplicate instruction, yielding 16,800 scheduled generations. They measure: (1) a deterministic All-8 diagnostic (passing eight observable tests of instruction following), (2) pre-provisional TF-IDF recall of relevant content, (3) final-answer accuracy, (4) premature commitment rate (answering too early), and (5) a blinded human challenge audit of perceived faithfulness. They also integrate duplication into an Answer Engineering (AE) framework, where model trajectories are used for local repair, and compare several endpoints with and without duplication.
AI.result: Moving from one to two copies of the procedural instruction improves the All-8 diagnostic from 90.22% to 93.17%, eliminating about 30.2% of the remaining failures after one copy. TF-IDF recall increases modestly from 73.44% to 74.81% with strong statistical significance (Holm-adjusted p < .001). Final-answer accuracy stays unchanged at 60.21%, showing that duplication mainly affects process reliability rather than correctness of the final choice. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536), indicating a slight increase in early answering. In a blinded challenge audit, they obtain 10/30 directional confirmations and 20/30 ties, with no reversals, but fail to meet a prespecified 28/30 confirmation threshold. When combined with Answer Engineering, duplication raises an SSNHL endpoint from 84.2% to 97.1% (compared with an earlier published 25.1% no-editing baseline) and yields 73.8% for a conductive diagnostic branch-preservation endpoint versus 78.6% with AE alone and 58.9% with the original no-editing baseline.
AI.conclusion: Instruction duplication is a simple, low-complexity, black-box inference-time control that can measurably improve procedural instruction following and trajectory quality without affecting final-answer accuracy. Its benefits are placement-sensitive and modest at the raw model level, but can translate into substantial operational gains when a downstream system (such as Answer Engineering) consumes and repairs the model’s reasoning trajectory. However, there are tradeoffs, such as slightly increased premature commitment, and not all evaluative criteria (e.g., the blinded audit’s prespecified confirmation threshold) are met, indicating that duplication is a useful but not sufficient solution for robust controllable behavior.

title: The Impact of Synthetic Data Augmentation on Discourse-Pragmatic Function Classification
summary: Synthetic data augmentation has become a common strategy for addressing class imbalance in NLP, but most approaches focus on the quantity and diversity of generated examples rather than their geometric relationship to real training data. We investigate this question in the context of discourse pragmatic function classification, a task where data sparsity is a structural feature rather than a collection artefact. Using 410 manually annotated instances of the English word look drawn from the British National Corpus, spanning four functions: Attention Signal, Directive, Discourse Marker, and Interjection. We generate synthetic training examples with Llama 3.1 and partition them by their cosine distance from real training data in RoBERTa embedding space. We compare six training conditions that differ in the placement of synthetic examples relative to the empirical decision boundary, while holding augmentation quantity constant across conditions. All augmented conditions improve macro F and accuracy over the real only baseline, but core proximal examples (NEAR) yield the largest gains in macro F (0.113), while a distance balanced mix achieves the highest accuracy (0.748). No condition improves AUC, indicating that augmentation shifts the decision boundary rather than improving the model's underlying probability estimates. These findings suggest that where synthetic examples land in representation space matters as much as how many are generated, with implications for low resource pragmatic classification more broadly.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the *location* of synthetic NLP data in embedding space (near vs far from real data) affects performance in a low-resource discourse pragmatic classification task, finding that proximity to real examples matters as much as quantity.
AI.motivation: While synthetic data augmentation is widely used to combat class imbalance in NLP, prior work largely optimizes for more and more diverse examples, not for their geometric position relative to real data in representation space. In discourse pragmatic function classification, data sparsity is inherent (due to low natural frequency and subtle functions), making it crucial to understand what kind of synthetic data is most beneficial. The authors aim to determine whether synthetic examples that are close to real examples (in embedding space) yield better improvements than those that are more distant, and how this affects decision boundaries and probability calibration.
AI.method: The authors focus on classifying the discourse pragmatic function of the English word "look" into four classes (Attention Signal, Directive, Discourse Marker, Interjection), using 410 manually annotated instances from the British National Corpus. They generate synthetic training examples for these classes using Llama 3.1. Each synthetic example is embedded using RoBERTa, and its cosine distance to real training examples is computed. Synthetic data are then partitioned into groups based on this distance (e.g., NEAR/core proximal vs farther regions). Six training conditions are constructed that differ only in where, in embedding space, the synthetic examples are drawn from relative to the empirical decision boundary; the total amount of augmentation is held constant. Models are trained under each condition, and performance is evaluated with macro-F1, accuracy, and AUC to characterize changes in classification performance and calibration.
AI.result: All augmented training conditions outperform a baseline trained only on real data in terms of macro-F1 and accuracy. Synthetic examples that are core proximal (NEAR) to real data in RoBERTa space provide the largest improvement in macro-F1 (an increase of 0.113 over the baseline), suggesting better performance across classes, including minority ones. A configuration that balances synthetic examples across distances (a distance-balanced mix) achieves the highest overall accuracy (0.748). However, none of the augmentation conditions improve AUC, indicating that the classifier's ranking of instances by predicted probability—and thus its calibration—does not improve. Augmentation appears mainly to shift the learned decision boundary rather than enhancing the underlying probability estimates.
AI.conclusion: The geometry of synthetic data in representation space—specifically, how close synthetic examples are to real examples and to the empirical decision boundary—substantially influences the effectiveness of data augmentation in low-resource discourse pragmatic classification. Proximal synthetic data are particularly beneficial for macro-F1, while a mix of distances can optimize accuracy, but these benefits do not extend to AUC or probability calibration. Therefore, it is not enough to simply generate large quantities of diverse synthetic examples; practitioners should consider where those examples land in embedding space when designing augmentation strategies, especially for structurally sparse, low-resource pragmatic tasks.

title: IRWOZ 2.0: A Large Language Model-driven Dialogue Dataset for Industrial Robot Conversations
summary: IRWOZ has improved industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems through domain-specific annotations. However, its initial version contains substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, limiting state-tracking accuracy. We introduce IRWOZ 2.0, which addresses these limitations through large language model (LLM) enhanced generation (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and quality refinements. Our improved dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), featuring manual corrections and automated typo removal. Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrate significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ. To support industrial HRI research, we publicly released IRWOZ 2.0 dataset at https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/irwoz-20-large-language-model-driven-dialogue-dataset-industrial-robot-conversations

AI.tldr: IRWOZ 2.0 is a cleaner, expanded industrial human-robot dialogue dataset that significantly improves dialogue state tracking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The initial IRWOZ dataset for industrial human-robot interaction contained substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, which hurt dialogue state-tracking performance. A cleaner, higher-quality, and larger domain-specific dataset is needed to better support research and development of robust HRI dialogue systems.
AI.method: The authors construct IRWOZ 2.0 by using large language models (Mistral and Claude-3.5) to enhance dialogue generation, followed by quality refinement steps. They expand the dataset to 390 dialogues across four industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), apply manual corrections to dialogue content and states, and use automated tools for typo removal. They then benchmark dialogue state tracking performance (e.g., with GPT-2) on the new dataset versus the original IRWOZ.
AI.result: IRWOZ 2.0 provides 390 dialogues spanning four industrial domains with improved annotations and reduced noise. Benchmark experiments show substantially better dialogue state tracking performance: for example, GPT-2’s BLEU-4 score increases from 0.1651 on the original IRWOZ to 0.5604 on IRWOZ 2.0, indicating much higher alignment between predicted and reference dialogue states/utterances.
AI.conclusion: IRWOZ 2.0 is a higher-quality, LLM-enhanced, and expanded dialogue dataset for industrial human-robot interaction that significantly improves benchmark performance for dialogue state tracking. Its public release aims to support and accelerate research in industrial HRI dialogue systems.

title: Enhancing Financial Question Answering: A Novel Benchmark Dataset of Banks' financial statements
summary: The comparative analysis of banks' financial statements poses significant challenges for automated question answering systems due to their complexity, substantial length, technical language, and inhomogeneity of both textual and numerical content across different jurisdictions and institutions. We introduce FinRAG-QA, a novel benchmark dataset for financial question answering, which comprises 999 practitioner-curated questions on 10 standardised indicators, grounded in 209 annual and Pillar 3 reports from 24 major European and U.S. banks spanning 2019-2023. Unlike prior financial QA benchmarks, which centre on U.S. filings and single-institution analysis, FinRAG-QA targets cross-institutional retrieval over documents averaging 198k words, longer than any existing financial QA resource. On this benchmark we evaluate a multi-stage RAG pipeline and isolate the contribution of each component. Contextual chunk enrichment combined with a retrieval-optimised embedding model raises NDCG@10 from 0.322 to 0.710; conditional on the ground truth being retrieved, a reasoning-optimised generator raises answer accuracy from 44.6% to 79.0% (+34.4 percentage points), at roughly 20x the generation latency. We further show that cross-encoder reranking degrades retrieval when the first-stage ranking is already strong, and that a single top-ranked chunk outperforms larger contexts at generation time. Experiments were run in late 2024-early 2025 with the models available at that time.

AI.tldr: FinRAG-QA is a new large-scale cross-bank financial QA benchmark based on long annual and Pillar 3 reports, used to dissect and optimise a multi-stage RAG pipeline for retrieval and reasoning over complex financial disclosures.
AI.motivation: Automated QA over banks’ financial statements is hard because reports are extremely long, use specialised terminology, and mix heterogeneous text and numbers across institutions and jurisdictions. Existing QA benchmarks mostly cover U.S. single-firm filings and much shorter documents, so they do not adequately test cross-institution retrieval and reasoning at realistic scale. The authors want a benchmark that reflects real practitioners’ information needs and allows systematic evaluation of RAG components in this demanding setting.
AI.method: The authors construct FinRAG-QA, a benchmark with 999 expert-written questions about 10 standardised financial indicators, anchored in 209 annual and Pillar 3 reports from 24 large European and U.S. banks between 2019–2023. They then build a multi-stage retrieval-augmented generation pipeline and perform ablation-style experiments: varying chunking and contextual enrichment, using a retrieval-optimised embedding model, adding or removing cross-encoder reranking, and testing different context sizes for the generator. They also compare base vs reasoning-optimised generators and measure metrics such as NDCG@10 for retrieval and answer accuracy, including conditional on retrieving the ground-truth evidence.
AI.result: FinRAG-QA documents average 198k words, exceeding the length of prior financial QA resources and enabling realistic cross-bank comparisons. In experiments, enriching chunks with context plus switching to a retrieval-optimised embedding model improves NDCG@10 from 0.322 to 0.710. Given that the correct evidence is retrieved, a reasoning-focused LLM boosts answer accuracy from 44.6% to 79.0%, but with around 20x higher latency. Cross-encoder reranking, when applied on top of an already strong first-stage retriever, actually worsens retrieval quality. Using only the single top-ranked chunk as input for generation yields better answers than feeding larger multi-chunk contexts.
AI.conclusion: FinRAG-QA provides a challenging, practitioner-grounded benchmark for QA over long, heterogeneous bank disclosures and enables fine-grained study of RAG systems in this domain. Effective QA requires both improved retrieval—via enriched chunks and specialised embeddings—and stronger reasoning models, but there is a latency–accuracy trade-off. Some common practices, like cross-encoder reranking and very large context windows at generation time, may be counterproductive when first-stage retrieval is strong and the top evidence chunk is already highly informative.

title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a bias in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) where lucky guesses are over-rewarded, and proposes SIGNBALANCE, a modified advantage estimator that removes dependence on rollout composition while preserving verifier feedback, leading to better performance on tasks prone to guessing.
AI.motivation: GRPO is popular for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (e.g., math problems with checkable answers) because it can leverage group-based reward statistics. However, the current advantage estimator can’t distinguish between trajectories that reached the correct answer by genuine reasoning and those that arrived there by chance guessing. In settings with small answer spaces, bounded subcases, or many search paths, this causes a “spurious advantage” that encourages guessing-like policies, degrading the quality and robustness of learned reasoning. The authors aim to correct this bias without sacrificing the benefits of GRPO.
AI.method: The authors analytically identify conditions under which GRPO’s within-group advantage estimator becomes spuriously high for guess-based rollouts. They categorize problem regimes where this happens: (1) tasks with small bounded answer sets, (2) open-answer tasks with bounded sub-cases, and (3) search agents with large budgets that induce many paths to the same answer. To address this, they propose SIGNBALANCE, an alternative advantage estimator that: (a) preserves only the verifier’s sign (correct vs incorrect), (b) uses a global scaling factor rather than within-group magnitudes, and (c) enforces zero-mean balance via per-class (e.g., correct/incorrect) rescaling with stop-gradient so that the re-centering doesn’t leak gradients through the group statistics. This design makes the magnitude independent of how the answer was reached (composition-free) while keeping the learning signal aligned with correctness.
AI.result: On benchmarks covering math reasoning and search-agent settings at different model scales, SIGNBALANCE performs on par with standard GRPO in open-answer math tasks where guessing is less problematic, and significantly outperforms GRPO in bounded-answer math tasks and search-agent setups where spurious advantage from guessing is more severe. The experiments show that SIGNBALANCE reduces the tendency of the policy to adopt guess-like behavior while maintaining or improving final performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that GRPO’s standard advantage estimator systematically over-rewards lucky guesses in several common problem regimes, leading to a spurious learning signal. SIGNBALANCE, by using sign-only verification, global scaling, and balanced per-class rescaling with stop-gradient, eliminates this spurious advantage while keeping the core benefits of verifiable-reward RL. Empirically, it preserves GRPO’s strengths on open-ended tasks and yields clear gains on bounded-answer and search-heavy tasks. The authors position SIGNBALANCE as a drop-in replacement for GRPO’s advantage estimator for verifiable-reward RL, especially where guessing is prevalent.

title: A Circuit for Plural Reference: How LLMs Represent and Retrieve Singular and Plural Entities
summary: Coreference resolution is an important task in contextual reasoning. In this paper, we investigate the mechanism for representing and retrieving singular and plural entities for plural reference. We use a combination of mechanistic interpretability and attention pattern analysis to study the process in which LLMs predict a pronoun to refer back to previously mentioned entities. Using a range of causal intervention techniques, we find a set of attention heads that are responsible for (1) representing coreference information in the input, (2) identifying entities that form a plural reference, (3) transferring the information to the component that is responsible for selecting the antecedents and predicting the pronoun. We also find that LLMs align with humans in preference for plural pronoun. Specifically, entities in a plural construction are more likely to be referred to as a plural entity if they are ontologically similar and are linked by the conjunction "and".

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how LLMs handle coreference for plural pronouns using mechanistic interpretability and attention analysis.
AI.motivation: To understand the internal mechanisms by which LLMs represent and retrieve singular and plural entities when resolving plural pronouns, and to compare these mechanisms with human preferences.
AI.method: Apply mechanistic interpretability, attention pattern analysis, and causal intervention techniques to identify attention heads involved in representing coreference information, grouping entities into plural references, and passing this information to components that select antecedents and predict pronouns.
AI.result: A set of attention heads is identified with distinct roles: representing coreference info in the input, detecting entities that form a plural reference, and routing this information to pronoun-prediction components. The model’s behavior shows alignment with human preferences for when plural pronouns are used.
AI.conclusion: LLMs implement a structured, decomposable mechanism for plural coreference that partly mirrors human preferences: they are more likely to treat entities as a plural unit when those entities are ontologically similar and joined by the conjunction “and.”

title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DRACO, a method to turn trajectory-level rubric scores into informative per-step advantages for RL agents in outcome-blind, long-horizon tasks, yielding better performance than both sparse ground-truth rewards and prior rubric-based methods.
AI.motivation: Many real-world, long-horizon RL tasks lack programmatic success checkers, making reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inapplicable. In these outcome-blind settings, human- or rubric-based trajectory evaluations are common, but they provide only a single scalar score per long trajectory, which is a weak and sparse learning signal. There is a need for a principled method to convert high-level, multi-criteria rubric evaluations into rich, step-level credit assignment signals that can effectively guide policy optimization without relying on environment verifiers or trained attribution models.
AI.method: The authors propose DRACO (Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization). During training, the system dynamically generates multi-criteria rubrics that adapt to the evolving capabilities of the policy. For each completed trajectory, these rubrics are evaluated once to obtain rubric-specific scores. DRACO then analytically redistributes the resulting trajectory-level judgments back over individual steps associated with each rubric item, producing differentiated per-step advantages suitable for use in GRPO (a policy optimization algorithm). The redistribution is done via a closed-form credit assignment scheme that avoids learning an additional attribution network, ensuring efficiency and stability.
AI.result: On the AppWorld benchmark, DRACO improves performance by 15.9 points over the base model and by 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite DRACO itself not using any programmatic verifiers. On the out-of-domain Tau-Bench benchmark, DRACO gains 5.3 points over the base model even in the absence of a frontier judge, and it outperforms both ground-truth-reward-based training and alternative rubric-based training baselines. These results indicate that redistributed rubric advantages provide a stronger learning signal than sparse outcome rewards and prior rubric usage schemes.
AI.conclusion: DRACO demonstrates that dynamically generated rubrics, combined with a closed-form redistribution of trajectory-level rubric scores into per-step advantages, can significantly enhance RL training in outcome-blind, long-horizon tasks. By avoiding verifiers and learned attribution modules, it remains broadly applicable and computationally efficient, while empirically surpassing both ground-truth-reward training and previous rubric-based methods on challenging benchmarks. The approach suggests that well-designed rubric redistribution is a powerful substitute for explicit environmental success signals in complex agent training settings.

title: Opening mind by opening architecture: analysis strategies
comment: Presented at the 7th International Csound Conference (ICSC 2024), Vienna, September 2024
summary: In numerical signal processing for electroacoustic composition, the progressive loss of specific development and research environments caused by the increasing use of digital market tools has favoured the dominance of the closed-architecture audio processor model. This model, while powerful, envisions the possibility of describing output data about its perceived characteristics, but at the cost of ignoring its internal process and interacting systems, which become complex, powerful environments but closed in an inscrutable black box, a loss we must consider. Any digital signal processing technique tells a story. Just as the words of a language incorporate social, historical and technical polysemic layers, a signal processor has its own story of implementation, a gradual technological achievement with its inevitable aesthetic consequences. Through the looking-glass of literature, one can access those environments with renewed awareness by reestablishing a scientific method and an attitude to research. In this specific case, starting from the case study of Manfred Schroeder's historical reverbs, we illustrate the process of building analytical evaluation tools, as well as practical implementation, at the basis of a conscious study path.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques the dominance of closed-architecture audio processors in electroacoustic composition and advocates for analytically reconstructing and re-implementing classic signal processing tools (like Schroeder reverbs) to recover their technical and aesthetic 'stories.'
AI.motivation: The authors are concerned that the shift to commercial, closed-architecture digital audio tools has obscured the inner workings, histories, and aesthetic implications of signal processing methods used in electroacoustic music. They want to restore awareness of how these tools function and evolve, arguing that each DSP algorithm embodies a technological and artistic narrative that is lost when treated as a black box.
AI.method: They conceptually and practically revisit historical digital reverberation algorithms by Manfred Schroeder as a case study. Using a literature-informed, research-oriented approach, they develop analytical evaluation tools and practical implementations to open up the internal processes of these reverbs. This involves reconstructing, analyzing, and re-implementing the algorithms to make their behavior and design principles transparent.
AI.result: The work yields a set of analytical evaluation tools and practical implementations of Schroeder-style reverbs that make their internal processes and design choices visible and examinable. This supports a more conscious, research-based approach to using and teaching DSP in electroacoustic composition, highlighting the link between technical design and aesthetic outcome.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that treating DSP techniques as transparent, analyzable systems—rather than black-box tools—enriches both technical understanding and artistic practice in electroacoustic composition. By reconstructing and studying classic algorithms like Schroeder’s reverbs, composers and researchers can regain a critical, historically informed relationship to their tools, fostering more deliberate and reflective creative work.

title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
summary: Hybrid LLMs pair softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), whose recurrent state summarizes the context in fixed size. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers) left the GDN block in 8- or 16-bit precision -- especially its decay and write-strength gates -- on the intuition that errors in a recurrence accumulate over long contexts. We test that intuition by building Minima: NVFP4 W4A4 on all 496 linear layers, GDN included. Across perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K, Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) recipe we compare, and its 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism study explains why: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes the residual stream's extreme outliers, equalizing activation error across layer roles; (ii) the supposedly fragile gate projections are the least sensitive -- softplus/exponential and sigmoid parameterizations compress ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps, because each write overwrites the state along the current key direction; (iv) the per-token quantization cost washes out with context instead of compounding. We also repair a global-scale mismatch that arises when per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints are served by kernels that fuse those modules into one GEMM, and show calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free. The result: a practical recipe -- quantize everything, ship KV scales -- and a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easy half to quantize. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Minima, a fully 4-bit-quantized hybrid LLM (including all linear recurrent layers) that matches BF16 accuracy while being smaller and faster.
AI.motivation: Hybrid LLMs with both softmax attention and linear recurrent blocks like Gated DeltaNet offer long-context efficiency, but are expensive to serve. Community 4-bit quantizations kept the recurrent GDN layers at higher precision due to fears that quantization noise would accumulate over long recurrences. This limited memory and speed gains. The authors want to test whether this intuition is necessary and find a principled, practical recipe for aggressively quantizing the recurrent part without losing quality.
AI.method: They build a Qwen3.8-27B variant named Minima where all 496 linear layers, including GDN gates, use NVFP4 W4A4 quantization. They benchmark it against BF16 and other recipes on perplexity at 4K/32K and several reasoning, coding, retrieval, and knowledge tasks. They then conduct a four-part mechanistic study: (i) analyzing how NVFP4’s block-wise scaling interacts with residual outliers; (ii) measuring sensitivity of gate projections and how nonlinearities compress GEMM errors; (iii) injecting noise/impulses into the GDN delta-rule recurrence to track error propagation and forgetting over long sequences; and (iv) characterizing how per-token quantization error behaves with context length. They also diagnose and fix a global-scale mismatch from serving per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints with fused kernels and explore FP8 KV-cache scaling.
AI.result: Minima (fully NVFP4 W4A4, including GDN) matches BF16 within run-to-run seed noise across benchmarks (average score difference -0.52 over five tasks), while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and having 14–19% faster prefill. Its 32K-token perplexity gap with BF16 shrinks with position, indicating no runaway error accumulation. Mechanistic experiments show: (i) NVFP4’s 16-element block scaling isolates extreme residual outliers, evening out activation quantization error; (ii) gate projections are actually robust, with nonlinear parameterizations shrinking ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence keeps noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and quickly forgets state impulses due to overwrite along current key directions; and (iv) per-token quantization error averages out with context rather than compounding. They also resolve scale mismatches in fused kernels and demonstrate that calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales do not hurt performance.
AI.conclusion: The recurrent half of hybrid LLMs, including GDN-style linear layers, is easier to quantize than previously assumed: errors do not accumulate catastrophically over long contexts. With NVFP4 W4A4 on all linear layers plus calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales and proper handling of fused kernels, one can "quantize everything" and still match BF16 quality while improving speed and memory. This provides both a practical deployment recipe and a mechanistic explanation for the robustness of recurrent components to aggressive quantization.

title: Beyond BLEU: A Case for Redefining Sign Language Translation Benchmarks
summary: BLEU-4 is the standard metric for evaluating sign language translation (SLT), but spoken-language metrics may not adequately reflect sign language proficiency. The multimodal, low-resource context of SLT allows models to exploit spurious correlations and spoken-language priors, rather than learning stronger sign representations. In this paper, we evaluate the relationship between spatio-temporal understanding and BLEU-4 across six SLT models on Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily, showing that gains in BLEU-4 are not on their own evidence of better sign language understanding. This work introduces an alternative inspired by language-learning assessment, using an open-weight-LLM QA protocol that measures salient content preservation. It aligns more closely with human rankings and is six to seven times more paraphrase-invariant than BLEU-4. Applied to SLT, this protocol targets content transfer, is more robust to train-test overlap, and gives a different picture of the field: the five gloss-free systems are largely within noise of one another on Phoenix-2014T, while the gloss-supervised system stands 9.3 points higher, a gap invisible to BLEU-4.

AI.tldr: BLEU-4, the standard metric for sign language translation (SLT), does not reliably reflect true sign-language understanding; an LLM-based QA evaluation focused on content preservation correlates better with humans and reveals performance gaps hidden by BLEU-4.
AI.motivation: Current SLT evaluation relies almost exclusively on BLEU-4, a metric designed for spoken-language MT. In multimodal, low-resource SLT, models can exploit dataset artifacts and spoken-language priors to improve BLEU-4 without genuinely learning rich spatio-temporal sign representations. The authors are motivated by the need for an evaluation method that better captures semantic understanding of sign content and aligns with human judgments, while being robust to paraphrasing and train-test overlap.
AI.method: The authors analyze six SLT models on two benchmarks (Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily), probing the relationship between BLEU-4 scores and spatio-temporal understanding. They then propose an alternative evaluation protocol inspired by language-learning assessment: an open-weight LLM-based question-answering (QA) setup that measures preservation of salient content in translations. This protocol is evaluated for paraphrase invariance, correlation with human rankings, robustness to train-test overlap, and its ability to differentiate between gloss-free and gloss-supervised systems.
AI.result: They find that improvements in BLEU-4 do not consistently indicate better spatio-temporal understanding of sign language. The proposed LLM-QA protocol correlates more strongly with human rankings and is six to seven times more invariant to paraphrasing than BLEU-4. When applied to SLT systems, it shows that five gloss-free models perform similarly and are mostly indistinguishable within noise on Phoenix-2014T, while a gloss-supervised model scores 9.3 points higher under the new metric—a performance gap that BLEU-4 fails to reveal.
AI.conclusion: BLEU-4 is insufficient as a standalone metric for evaluating sign language translation quality and understanding. An LLM-based QA evaluation focused on salient content transfer provides a more semantically faithful, paraphrase-robust, and human-aligned measure of SLT performance, revealing meaningful performance differences—such as the advantage of gloss supervision—that BLEU-4 obscures.

title: Epistemic Warrant for LLM Recommendations: Characterizing the Basis for Reliance When Ground Truth Is Unavailable
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to support organizational decisions, yet users often lack a principled basis for assessing whether to rely on a specific recommendation. Existing approaches typically evaluate broad model properties, such as reliability, uncertainty, or robustness, or focus on user trust, rather than the underlying basis for relying on an individual recommendation. Adapting theoretical foundations from epistemology, we introduce epistemic warrant, a decision-level construct that characterizes the stability of a model's preference and the scope over which that preference holds. We operationalize this construct through a four-tier reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations, distinguishing among unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, and broadly supported recommendations. We validate the construct using contemporary methodologies: known-groups tests successfully recover expert-prespecified warrant orderings, and stronger warrants systematically align with independent consensus from crowd workers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that epistemic warrant provides information distinct from verbalized confidence and is not readily explained by decision difficulty. Ultimately, this framework offers a theoretically grounded, implementable approach for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and validates a practical framework to rate how much one should rely on a specific LLM recommendation when ground truth is unavailable, based on a new construct called epistemic warrant.
AI.motivation: Organizations increasingly use LLMs for consequential decisions, but current evaluation methods focus on global model properties or user trust rather than whether a specific recommendation is well founded. There is a need for a principled, decision-level way to judge when to rely on an individual LLM output, especially where no objective ground truth exists.
AI.method: The authors adapt concepts from epistemology to define “epistemic warrant,” capturing how stable a model’s preference is and how broadly that preference holds across variations of the decision context. They operationalize epistemic warrant as a four-level reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations: unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, and broadly supported. They then empirically validate this construct using known-groups tests against expert-specified warrant orderings, and compare warrant levels to independent judgments from crowd workers. They also test whether epistemic warrant is distinct from model verbalized confidence and from measures of decision difficulty.
AI.result: Known-groups experiments show that the proposed warrant levels recover expert-prespecified orderings of recommendation strength. Higher warrant levels reliably correspond to stronger agreement among independent crowd workers, supporting construct validity. Analyses indicate that epistemic warrant captures information not reducible to the model’s stated confidence or to how difficult the decision is, suggesting it is a distinct and informative property of recommendations.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic warrant is a useful decision-level construct for characterizing how well supported an individual LLM recommendation is when ground truth is unavailable. The four-tier reliance certificate is both theoretically grounded and practically implementable, providing organizations with a structured way to assess and communicate when and how much to rely on specific LLM outputs beyond general notions of trust or reliability.

title: Typological Feature Prediction with Large Language Models: An In-Context Learning Approach
summary: Typological features are widely used in multilingual NLP, and the prediction of such features holds downstream utility. However, existing methods to predict missing values lack interpretable justifications for predictions, while their performance across resource levels and feature types remains underexplored. Given LLMs' abilities in meta-linguistic reasoning and in providing rationales, we investigate LLMs' performance in typological feature prediction via an in-context learning approach with linguistic data from URIEL+ and Glottolog. We find that zero-shot prompting is insufficient, but when given phylogenetic and geographic neighbour evidence, LLMs substantially outperform all baselines without disadvantaging low-resource languages. We further find that most LLM rationales are consistent with the provided evidence, offering a step toward explainable typological feature prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates large language models for predicting linguistic typological features, showing that with context from related languages, they outperform prior methods while giving interpretable rationales.
AI.motivation: Typological features are crucial for multilingual NLP tasks, but many languages lack complete annotations and existing prediction approaches do not explain their decisions well and are not well understood across different resource settings and feature types. With LLMs now capable of meta-linguistic reasoning and generating explanations, it is important to assess whether they can improve typological feature prediction and provide justifiable, interpretable rationales.
AI.method: The authors use an in-context learning setup with large language models, feeding them typological and genealogical information from URIEL+ and Glottolog for a target language along with evidence from its phylogenetic and geographic neighbours. They compare zero-shot prompting versus prompts augmented with neighbour evidence, evaluate performance against baseline typology prediction methods, and analyze the consistency of LLM-generated rationales with the given evidence across different resource levels and feature types.
AI.result: Zero-shot prompting of the LLMs performs poorly for typological feature prediction. However, when the models are given evidence from phylogenetic and geographic neighbours, they significantly outperform all baseline methods while maintaining performance for low-resource languages. Additionally, qualitative and/or quantitative analysis shows that most of the explanations produced by the LLMs align with the supplied neighbour evidence.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, when properly prompted with evidence from related languages, are effective tools for predicting missing typological features and surpass traditional baselines, without introducing biases against low-resource languages. Their rationales generally reflect the evidence they are given, making this approach a promising step toward more explainable and trustworthy typological feature prediction in multilingual NLP.

title: Environment Evolution for Terminal Agents
summary: Scaling interactive and verifiable environments is critical for training terminal agents. As frontier models become more capable, environments synthesized from scratch become less challenging and thus provide limited learning signals. Recent co-evolution methods iteratively synthesize environments near the model's learnable frontier based on weaknesses exposed during rollouts. However, their dependence on on-policy rollouts limits generalization and the continuous provision of learning signals as the model becomes stronger. In this paper, we propose environment evolution, which incrementally increases environment difficulty off-policy and schedules the evolved environments generation by generation during training to provide continuous learning signals. We derive three evolution directions that influence environment difficulty from the multi-turn learning objective and then implement evolution along these directions through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness. Quantitative rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol show that environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments. We validate its effectiveness on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B through simple long-horizon RL training, improving their performance by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an off-policy environment evolution framework that automatically makes interactive terminal environments harder over generations, enabling stronger and more continuous training signals for terminal agents.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based terminal agents improve, environments that are synthesized from scratch become too easy and stop providing useful learning signals. Existing co-evolution methods try to adapt by generating new environments near the model’s competence frontier, but they depend on on-policy rollouts from the current model, which limits generalization and makes it hard to keep providing challenging tasks as the model becomes stronger. There is a need for a scalable way to automatically increase environment difficulty in a principled, off-policy manner so agents can continue to learn effectively over long horizons.
AI.method: The authors introduce an environment evolution framework that gradually increases the difficulty of terminal-style interactive environments off-policy and schedules them generation-by-generation during training. They derive three concrete evolution directions from a formal multi-turn learning objective—these directions define how to modify environments to be more challenging while still solvable. They then implement these evolution directions within a loop-engineered multi-agent harness that uses strong LLMs (Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) to synthesize and transform environments across generations. The evolved environments are then used in a simple long-horizon RL training setup for target models.
AI.result: Rollout experiments using strong LLMs as evaluation agents show that environments produced by the evolution framework are consistently more difficult than the initial ones. When training Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with the evolved environments under a straightforward long-horizon RL scheme, the models achieve substantial gains on the Terminal-Bench 2.1 benchmark: +14.4 and +18.0 percentage points, respectively, compared to their baselines without environment evolution.
AI.conclusion: Environment evolution, as an off-policy, generation-wise approach to automatically increasing environment difficulty, can effectively maintain and amplify learning signals for terminal agents. By deriving principled evolution directions and realizing them with a multi-agent harness, the method produces progressively harder yet solvable environments and yields significant performance gains on a standard terminal benchmark. This suggests that structured environment evolution is a promising direction for scaling interactive training of advanced terminal agents beyond what static or purely on-policy co-evolution methods can provide.

title: IndicSafeEval: Safety Robustness of Large Language Models under Multilingual Persuasive Jailbreak Attacks
comment: 38 pages, 7 figures, 33 tables. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. Contains examples of harmful model outputs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multilingual settings, yet their safety is still evaluated primarily in English. This limits our understanding of how alignment failures manifest in low-resource and culturally diverse languages. We introduce IndicSafeEval, a persuasion-based jailbreak evaluation framework for Indian languages. Our benchmark combines ten safety critical content categories with six human-like persuasive strategies across four different Indian languages, such as Hindi, Bengali, Marathi and Punjabi, resulting in 7,200 adversarial prompts. We conduct a systematic black-box evaluation of several open-source LLMs to examine how their safety behaviour varies across languages, persuasion strategies, and risk categories. Our analysis shows that the model does not behave equally safely across all languages and prompt styles. Instead, safety performance depends strongly on both the languages used and the way a request is phrased using persuasive cues. We further observe that different risk categories exhibit different levels of vulnerability, with some types of harmful content being significantly more susceptible to persuasion-based jailbreaks than others. These findings reveal important limitations of current safety evaluations, which are largely English-centric, and underscore the need for multilingual and persuasion-aware benchmarking frameworks to more accurately assess real-world LLM safety. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/MonSaikat/IndicSafeEval. Warning: this paper contains example data that may be offensive or harmful.

AI.tldr: Introduces IndicSafeEval, a multilingual, persuasion-based jailbreak benchmark for evaluating LLM safety in four Indian languages, showing that safety behavior varies significantly by language, persuasive style, and risk category, revealing limitations of English-centric safety evaluations.
AI.motivation: Most LLM safety evaluations are conducted in English, which overlooks how alignment failures may appear in low-resource, culturally diverse languages. There is a specific gap in understanding how persuasive, jailbreak-style prompts in Indian languages affect model safety. The authors aim to systematically study multilingual safety vulnerabilities, especially for Indian languages, under realistic, human-like persuasion strategies.
AI.method: The authors build IndicSafeEval, a benchmark that combines ten safety-critical risk categories with six human-like persuasive strategies across four Indian languages (Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Punjabi), generating 7,200 adversarial prompts. They then perform black-box evaluations of multiple open-source LLMs on this benchmark, measuring how often models comply with or resist unsafe requests. They analyze performance patterns across languages, persuasion strategies, and risk categories to quantify differential vulnerability.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that LLMs do not maintain uniform safety across languages or prompt formulations. Safety performance varies strongly based on the language and the persuasive strategy used. Some languages and persuasion styles more easily elicit unsafe responses. Additionally, different risk categories show distinct vulnerability levels, with some types of harmful content more prone to successful persuasion-based jailbreaks than others.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM safety assessments, which are predominantly English-focused and often ignore persuasion-based jailbreaks, give an incomplete picture of real-world safety. The results highlight the need for multilingual, persuasion-aware benchmarks such as IndicSafeEval to more accurately evaluate and improve LLM safety, particularly for low-resource and culturally diverse languages.

title: The Natural Language Interaction Protocol and Standard for AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly being developed and deployed across organizations using heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. To realize their potential social and business impact, these agents must be able to interoperate through a common communication protocol. The Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP), developed by researchers and practitioners across companies and universities and standardized by Ecma International, addresses this need by defining a standards-based application-layer protocol for AI-agent interaction. NLIP provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that can be carried over existing transports such as HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, and AMQP, while allowing NLIP-aware agents and gateways to adapt between clients, agents, local context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols. This paper presents the motivation and design rationale of NLIP, its message model and transport bindings, security-by-design considerations, reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and relationship to emerging agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NLIP, a standardized, lightweight natural-language interaction protocol that enables heterogeneous AI agents and systems to interoperate over existing transports like HTTP, WebSocket, and AMQP.
AI.motivation: AI agents are being built on diverse frameworks, models, tools, and infrastructures, which makes it hard for them to communicate and collaborate. Organizations need a common, interoperable protocol so agents from different vendors and environments can work together reliably and securely at scale.
AI.method: The authors design NLIP as an application-layer interaction protocol, specifying a semantic message envelope, message model, and bindings to common transports (HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, AMQP). They incorporate security-by-design principles, define how NLIP-aware agents and gateways interface with tools, context stores, and services, and provide a reference implementation plus example applications. They also analyze NLIP’s relationship to other emerging agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.
AI.result: NLIP offers a concrete, standards-based specification—adopted and standardized by Ecma International—for packaging and exchanging semantic messages between AI agents and related components. The reference implementation and early applications show that heterogeneous agents and enterprise services can interoperate through NLIP, and early adoption signals suggest growing ecosystem support.
AI.conclusion: A common, standards-backed protocol like NLIP can serve as a unifying interaction layer for AI agents, enabling interoperable, secure, and flexible communication across varied tools, models, and infrastructures. NLIP’s design, standardization, and early adoption position it as a key candidate for foundational infrastructure in emerging agent ecosystems and complement, rather than replace, other agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.

title: Evaluating Criterion-Conditioned Behaviour of Large Language Models in Content Moderation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong performance on standard content moderation benchmarks. However, these benchmarks often aggregate multiple moderation criteria into a single label, making it unclear whether models can disentangle them and reliably apply each criterion when making decisions. To study whether LLMs exhibit criterion-conditioned behaviour, we introduce Diagnostic Evaluation of COntent (DECO), a criterion-independent factorisation of content that enables controlled, criterion-level evaluation. We also introduce pairwise evaluation to compare model outputs across different criteria for the same input. Across four moderation datasets and four LLMs, we find that strong benchmark performance can hide substantial failures at the criterion level. Models struggle most when correct decisions depend not on overall harmfulness, but on the specific aspect of the content that the criterion requires them to assess. Our results highlight a key limitation of current content moderation benchmarks: strong performance on aggregated labels does not provide sufficient evidence that LLMs can reliably evaluate content with respect to individual moderation criteria. These findings call for the development of evaluation methods that explicitly measure criterion-conditioned behaviour.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models that look good on standard moderation benchmarks actually fail at reliably applying specific moderation criteria, and introduces a new evaluation framework (DECO) to reveal these weaknesses.
AI.motivation: Existing content moderation benchmarks typically collapse multiple moderation criteria (e.g., hate, harassment, self-harm) into a single aggregate label. This makes it impossible to know whether LLMs truly understand and can separately apply each criterion, or if they are just approximating overall harmfulness. There is a need to determine whether LLMs can condition their judgements on specific moderation rules, because real-world moderation requires fine-grained and criterion-specific decisions.
AI.method: The authors propose DECO (Diagnostic Evaluation of COntent), which factorises content into criterion-independent components so that the same input can be evaluated under different, clearly separated moderation criteria. They perform controlled, criterion-level evaluations across four moderation datasets and four LLMs. Additionally, they use pairwise evaluation: for the same piece of content, they compare model decisions across different criteria to see whether the models change their judgement appropriately when the applicable rule changes.
AI.result: Despite strong performance on standard, aggregated moderation benchmarks, LLMs show substantial failures when evaluated at the level of individual criteria. The models perform worst when correct decisions hinge not on generic harmfulness but on correctly identifying the particular aspect of the content that a given criterion targets. This reveals inconsistencies and misalignments in how models apply different moderation rules to the same content.
AI.conclusion: High scores on existing, aggregated content moderation benchmarks are misleading indicators of LLM reliability: they do not guarantee that a model can accurately and consistently apply specific moderation criteria. The paper concludes that new evaluation methods are needed—like DECO and pairwise, criterion-level testing—that explicitly measure criterion-conditioned behaviour to better assess and improve LLM-based content moderation systems.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Human-AI Interaction
summary: AI agents are trained on population-scale data to encode broad capabilities spanning those of many practitioners. Yet the artifacts they produce rarely meet the personal bar professionals need to stake their reputation on. On realistic, open-ended tasks where success criteria are heterogeneous and insufficiently documented, individual expertise lives precisely in the elevation and departure from the average. In practice, iterative human-agent interaction surfaces criteria that users cannot fully specify up front, yet apply repeatedly across tasks. We argue this cross-session interaction data is a rich, underused signal for closing the gap to individual expertise. In this work, we propose test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI), which integrates these signals into agent context and weights, and crystallizes each user's training and evaluation criteria via an evolving rubric module. We adapt agents to 30 individuals in two high-utility domains, writing and visual creation, on a total of 600 tasks. Our agents improve solo task success by 4.5-20.9% within only tens of tasks. Meanwhile, our evolving rubric module serves as a scalable annotation tool, creating evaluation rubrics that catch 16.0-22.3% more failures than those from LMs or humans alone. While agents are adapted towards individuals, we show these personalized agents also produce improvements in success of up to 8.8% that generalize across users.

AI.tldr: They introduce a method (TAHI) that personalizes AI agents to individual users through ongoing interaction at test time, improving task performance and automatically generating better evaluation rubrics.
AI.motivation: General-purpose AI agents are trained on broad population data, so they tend to produce “average” outputs that are often below what professionals require to trust and use them. In complex, open-ended tasks like writing and visual design, experts care about nuanced, personal criteria that are not fully specified in advance and are applied repeatedly across tasks. Current systems underuse the rich information in users’ iterative feedback and behavior across many sessions, which could bridge the gap between generic capability and individual expertise.
AI.method: They propose TAHI (test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction), where the agent is adapted to each user based on interaction logs collected during normal usage. The approach: (1) integrates cross-session interaction signals into the agent’s context and model weights; and (2) introduces an evolving rubric module that incrementally captures each user’s personalized training and evaluation criteria as a rubric. This rubric is updated over time from human-agent interactions and is used both to steer the agent’s behavior and to evaluate outcomes. They test TAHI on 30 individuals in two domains, writing and visual creation, over 600 tasks in total.
AI.result: Across these 600 tasks, the personalized agents adapted with TAHI improve individual (solo) task success rates by 4.5–20.9% after only tens of tasks per user. The evolving rubric module, when used as an annotation tool, yields evaluation rubrics that detect 16.0–22.3% more failures than rubrics created only by language models or only by humans. Even though TAHI specializes models to individuals, the resulting personalized agents still offer gains that transfer to other users, with up to 8.8% improvement in success on cross-user evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Cross-session human-agent interaction data is a powerful, underexploited signal for aligning AI agents with individual expertise. The TAHI framework shows that adapting models at test time to each user—via both weight/context updates and an evolving rubric—can substantially boost success rates on realistic creative tasks, improve the quality of evaluation rubrics, and still yield benefits that generalize beyond the targeted individuals. This suggests a promising path for scalable personalization and evaluation of AI agents in professional workflows.

title: Beyond Shallow Alignment: How Post-Training Methods Determine Refusal Circuits And Steering Robustness
comment: 27 pages, accepted at EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: How do the methods used to train language models to refuse harmful requests shape how that refusal actually works inside the model? We compare three post-training methods - supervised fine-tuning, reasoning-augmented fine-tuning (training on reasoning chains that justify a safety decision), and preference optimization (ORPO) - across three architecturally distinct models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen3-8B). We find that training method, not just data, reshapes how refusal is computed internally: reasoning-augmented training consistently produces a distinct kind of refusal computation, visible across all three models, while architecture independently shapes internal structure and how reliably refusal can be steered. Most importantly, no method we study achieves all three properties we would want from safe alignment at once: refusal that isn't concentrated in a few fragile components, safety gains that don't cost general capability, and safety behavior correctable through small, targeted edits. We caution against treating current post-training methods as a solved, reliable defense, especially for security-critical use. Code and models are available in https://github.com/hoangcuongnguyen2001/Beyond-Shallow-Alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how different post-training methods for making language models refuse harmful requests affect the internal mechanisms of refusal, across three model architectures.
AI.motivation: To understand whether current safety post-training techniques (like supervised fine-tuning, reasoning-augmented fine-tuning, and preference optimization) actually lead to robust, well-distributed, and correctable safety mechanisms inside language models, rather than fragile or shallow refusal behaviors.
AI.method: The authors compare three post-training methods—standard supervised fine-tuning, reasoning-augmented fine-tuning that includes explicit safety-justifying reasoning chains, and preference optimization (ORPO)—applied to three different base LMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen3-8B). They then study how refusals are internally computed and represented, and how easy it is to steer or edit these behaviors, using interpretability and intervention analyses.
AI.result: They find that training method significantly reshapes the internal refusal computation beyond just the training data. Reasoning-augmented fine-tuning leads to a distinct, identifiable pattern of refusal computation in all three model families. Model architecture also independently affects internal structure and the reliability of steering refusal. However, none of the methods simultaneously achieves: (1) non-fragile, well-distributed refusal mechanisms, (2) safety gains without sacrificing general capability, and (3) safety behavior that can be fixed with small, targeted edits.
AI.conclusion: Current post-training safety methods (SFT, reasoning-augmented SFT, ORPO) should not be considered fully reliable defenses, especially in security-critical settings. Each method has trade-offs and fails to deliver all the desirable properties of robust, precise, and non-fragile safety alignment, so further research is needed on more principled and robust approaches.

title: Terminal-Universe: Turning Agent Trajectories into Scalable Terminal Environments
summary: As terminal-based code agents become prevalent, agent trajectories have accumulated at scale, while realistic, executable environments remain scarce. However, environments are what agent post-training actually requires: each can be re-queried into many verifiable tasks and provides execution feedback, whereas a trajectory is a single frozen demonstration. Rather than generating environments from scratch, we observe that the tool-execution history in existing trajectories exposes the structure and contents of the environments in which they ran, making it possible to reconstruct those environments from the trajectories themselves. Thus, we introduce Terminal-Universe, a framework which turns each trajectory into a reusable environment and explores it for synthesizing new tasks and continued interactions. Specifically, Terminal-Universe replays the file operations recorded in a trajectory to restore each file before the agent modified it, yielding a partial workspace; a completion agent then supplies the missing files and dependencies. On this recovered workspace, we both reconstruct the original intent task and synthesize entirely new ones. Besides, we also scale the tasks along two complementary axes: breadth and depth. For breadth, we mine directional dependency relations between related environments and synthesize cross-workspace queries spanning multiple codebases, as developers routinely do in real-world development. For depth, we extend the initial single-turn query into a multi-round session that captures iterative user feedback and requirement refinement via a user agent. Applied to public terminal agent trajectories, Terminal-Universe produces 37.3k task-sufficient environments. Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on this corpus improves single-round performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and multi-round performance on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4 by 13.8 points.

AI.tldr: Terminal-Universe reconstructs realistic, executable coding environments from existing terminal-agent trajectories and uses them to generate many reusable tasks for better post-training of code agents.
AI.motivation: There is a growing number of terminal-based code agent trajectories, but realistic, executable environments for training and evaluating these agents are scarce. Trajectories are single-use demonstrations, while environments can be reused to define many tasks and provide execution feedback. The authors want to leverage the rich information hidden in execution logs to overcome the data scarcity of realistic environments without needing to build them from scratch.
AI.method: The authors propose Terminal-Universe, a framework that converts each terminal-agent trajectory into a reusable environment. They: (1) Reconstruct a partial workspace by replaying the file operations recorded in the trajectory to restore files to their pre-modification state. (2) Use a completion agent to fill in missing files and dependencies, producing a task-sufficient environment. (3) Reconstruct the original intent task and synthesize new tasks on this recovered workspace.
